1.subtitle: The Great Indictment
1.intro: Overview. Isaiah begins not with comfort but with a courtroom. God summons heaven and earth as witnesses and places his own people in the dock. The charge is devastating: Israel, whom he raised and nurtured, has rebelled more thoroughly than a dumb animal ignores its owner. Chapter 1 is the book's overture: every major theme sounds here before the symphony begins. The depth of human guilt, the futility of religion without repentance, and the astonishing willingness of God to forgive — all three are stated before chapter 2 begins.

sections.title: The Indictment
sections.commentary:
God opens his case with a comparison that should have been impossible: the ox knows its owner, the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know its God. In the ancient world this was a mark of the deepest stupidity — the dumb animal grasps a relationship that God's covenant people have forgotten. The Reformers identified this as the root form of sin: not first immorality but the failure of the heart to treasure and trust its maker. Every other sin in Isaiah's catalogue grows from this soil.

v. 2 — “Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me.” The word rebelled (pasha) is the language of political revolt — a vassal breaking covenant with his sovereign. What God names first is not a list of sins but the posture behind them: the will turned in defiance against the one who gave it life.

Verses 5–6 paint the consequence as a body covered head to foot in untreated wounds. The damage is total and wilfully unaddressed. This is Isaiah's version of what Paul systematises in Romans 3: sin has corrupted every faculty. Yet verse 9 inserts a grace note that anchors everything: if any survivors remain at all, it is only because the LORD of hosts preserved them. Mercy is the only explanation for a remnant.

sections.title: Religion Without Repentance
sections.commentary:
God does not here condemn the sacrificial system — he instituted it. What he condemns is using religious activity as a substitute for transformed hearts. They were keeping the calendar, attending the feasts, multiplying their offerings — and God calls it an abomination. Why? Because their hands were full of blood (v. 15). The outward form had been severed from inward reality. This is the exact diagnosis Jesus levels at the Pharisees in Matthew 23: meticulous about tithes of mint, careless about justice and mercy.

v. 13 — “Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me.” The word vain (shav) means emptiness, falsehood. The offerings are not wrong in themselves; they are lying — claiming a devotion that does not exist. God would rather have silence than liturgy that misrepresents the heart.

Verse 18 arrives after this severity like sunlight through a storm, and its force depends entirely on what precedes it. “Come now, let us reason together” is a legal summons, not a gentle suggestion. God invites people whose hands are full of blood to stand in his courtroom and discover that his mercy outweighs their guilt. The scarlet and crimson will become snow and wool. R.C. Sproul called this one of the clearest gospel declarations in the Old Testament: total guilt, total cleansing, freely offered.

sections.title: The Faithful City and the Promise of Restoration
sections.commentary:
The lament of verse 21 is a love poem reversed. Jerusalem was made to be the city of God's glory — righteous, just, faithful. She has become a harlot. The image is painful precisely because the relationship was so intimate. God is not merely offended; he is grieved. The silver has become dross, the wine has been watered down.

The refining image of verse 25 is crucial: God will smelt away the dross. Judgment in Isaiah is rarely merely punitive; it is disciplinary and ultimately restorative. Keller draws attention to this pattern throughout the prophets: God uses hard providences to bring his people back to himself, not to destroy them. The silver is still there beneath the dross.

v. 27 — “Zion shall be redeemed by justice, and those in her who repent, by righteousness.” This is the theology of the whole book in miniature. Redemption does not come by overlooking sin but through justice satisfied — which ultimately points forward to the cross, where divine justice and mercy meet in the same act.

keyVerse.quote: “Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.”
keyVerse.note: This verse follows one of the most severe indictments in Scripture — which is precisely what gives it its force. The invitation is extended not to the respectable but to the guilty, not after improvement but before it. The transformation promised is not gradual but total: scarlet to snow, crimson to wool. God does not say ‘reform first, then I will reason with you.’ He says ‘come’ — and the coming is itself an act of grace enabling the response.

1.theology:
Grace and repentance. Chapter 1 holds together two things that feel contradictory: the totality of human guilt (vv. 2–8) and the totality of divine mercy (v. 18). The grace on offer is not the product of Israel's repentance — it is the invitation that makes repentance possible. God does not say “repent and then I will reason with you.” He says “come” first.

True worship. Verses 10–17 raise the question every generation must answer: what does God actually want from his people's worship? The answer is not fewer religious acts but hearts that correspond to the acts. The problem is not ceremony but integrity — form without substance, attendance without adoration.
1.reflection: Isaiah 1 confronts two persistent temptations simultaneously: the temptation to substitute religious activity for genuine heart-worship, and the temptation to despair at the depth of one's own guilt. The chapter exposes both — and verse 18 cuts through both at once. If you have ever thought your sin was too deep or too long-standing for grace, read verse 18 slowly, in the context of everything that precedes it.

2.subtitle: The Mountain of the LORD and the Day Against Pride
2.intro: Overview. Chapter 2 holds two visions in dramatic tension: the glorious future when all nations stream to Zion to learn God's ways (vv. 1–5), and the coming day when God levels everything proud and lofty (vv. 6–22). The chapter's governing refrain — the LORD alone will be exalted in that day — appears twice, staking out the theological conviction that drives everything: history is moving toward the exclusive exaltation of God, and everything that sets itself up in his place will be brought low before that day arrives.

sections.title: The Mountain of the LORD
sections.commentary:
The vision of verses 2–4 is one of the great eschatological passages of the Old Testament. In the latter days, the mountain of God's house will be established as the highest of mountains — not a geographical claim but a theological one: God's authority will be visibly supreme over every competing claim to human allegiance. Nations will not be forced to Zion; they will flow to it, drawn by the gravity of what is there.

v. 4 — “They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore.” The famous image is not naive pacifism but the consequence of a prior transformation: when all disputes are settled at God's throne, weapons of war become instruments of harvest. Peace is not achieved by disarmament; it comes from the reign of the Prince of Peace.

Verse 5 is the pivot from vision to application: “O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD.” The vision of the future is not meant to be admired from a distance; it is meant to change how God's people live now. Begg often notes this structure in the prophets: grand theology always lands in a personal call. The light is coming — so walk in it today.

sections.title: The Day of the LORD Against Pride
sections.commentary:
The contrast with the vision of verses 1–5 could not be sharper. There, nations stream up to God; here, people scramble down into caves to hide from him. The difference is entirely a matter of whether his appearing is welcomed or feared — and that depends on whether one has received his grace or resisted it.

The catalogue of verses 12–16 is deliberately comprehensive: cedars, oaks, mountains, towers, fortified walls, ships. Everything humanity builds its confidence upon has a day against it. God is not threatened by these things; he simply outranks them. Sproul called this one of the most important texts for understanding the holiness of God: the refrain the LORD alone will be exalted is the governing principle of all history.

v. 22 — “Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?” The most bracing command in the chapter. Cease putting ultimate confidence in human beings, however gifted or powerful. Even the greatest human leader is a creature dependent on the next breath. The only safe foundation is the one who will still be standing when the cedars have fallen.

keyVerse.quote: “The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.”
keyVerse.note: This phrase appears twice in the chapter (vv. 11 and 17), functioning as a refrain. Isaiah is not predicting that God will eventually win after a close contest. He is declaring that the exaltation of the LORD is the fixed destination of all history — and every human attempt at self-exaltation is moving against the tide of the universe.

2.theology:
The Day of the LORD. This concept — a decisive intervention of God to judge evil and establish his kingdom — runs throughout the prophets and into the New Testament. In Isaiah 2 it has a double edge: terror for the proud (vv. 10–22) and glory for those who stream to Zion (vv. 2–4). The same event produces both outcomes, depending entirely on whether one is under God's judgment or his grace.

Idolatry as pride. The idols of verses 8 and 20 are not simply bad religion; they are an expression of the deeper sin named in verse 22: the elevation of the human above the divine. Idolatry is pride in concrete form — the decision to trust the work of one's own hands rather than the God who made the hands.
2.reflection: The two halves of chapter 2 speak to the same reality from two angles. The vision of the nations streaming to Zion is meant to produce longing and hope. The vision of the day against pride is meant to produce sober self-examination. The question the chapter leaves ringing: where are you placing your confidence — in the things that will be brought low, or in the LORD who alone will be exalted?

3.subtitle: Judgment on Jerusalem's Leaders
3.intro: Overview. Chapter 3 works out a specific form of divine judgment: the withdrawal of good leadership. When God removes his blessing from a society, one of the earliest signs is the collapse of wise governance — boys become princes, the incompetent are elevated, the social order unravels from the top. The second half of the chapter turns to the women of Zion — not to single them out but because their pride and extravagance are a precise symptom of a society that has turned entirely inward, using wealth as a measure of worth while justice goes unsought.

sections.title: Leadership Stripped Away
sections.commentary:
God's judgment begins not as a foreign invasion but as a withdrawal. Support and supply, warrior and soldier, judge and prophet, elder and counsellor — all are removed. What remains is verse 4: boys as princes, infants as rulers. This is not a judgment on youth but on immaturity and the absence of wisdom that comes from fearing God. Leadership that is reactive, self-serving, and untethered from moral reality is itself a form of divine curse on a nation.

v. 9 — “They proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it.” There is a progression in moral decay: sin is first committed in secret, then tolerated, then normalised, then celebrated. When shamelessness itself becomes a virtue and the hiding instinct is gone, the society has moved beyond self-correction. MacArthur notes this is precisely the trajectory Paul traces in Romans 1.

The legal action of verse 13 — God rising to contend, standing to judge — is the backdrop for everything. The charge against the leaders is specific: you have devoured the vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses. Leaders who exploit the vulnerable will give account. The care of the poor appears throughout Isaiah as a mark of genuine covenant faithfulness.

vv. 10–11 — “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them… Woe to the wicked!” Tucked inside a chapter of unrelenting judgment, these two verses function as a pastoral anchor. They do not promise that the righteous will escape the chaos of a collapsing society. They declare ultimate outcomes. The moral universe God made has not been suspended.

sections.title: The Women of Zion
sections.commentary:
The extended passage on the women of Zion is frequently misread as prudishness about fashion. The point is different. Isaiah lists twenty-one items of luxury — anklets, headbands, crescents, perfume boxes, signet rings — painting a picture of a society that has turned its energy and imagination entirely toward self-adornment while the poor are ground down and justice is sold. The problem is not beauty; it is the idolatry of status, the use of wealth as the ultimate measure of worth.

The reversal of verse 24 is devastating in its symmetry: perfume replaced by rottenness, a belt by a rope, well-set hair by baldness, a rich robe by sackcloth, beauty by branding. The chapter ends in silence: “empty, she shall sit on the ground.” The city that adorned herself with finery ends stripped and silent. This is where every idolatrous substitute for God eventually arrives.

keyVerse.quote: “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him.”
keyVerse.note: These two verses in the middle of unrelenting judgment are a reminder that Isaiah's God is not random or arbitrary in his dealings. The moral universe holds. Whatever suffering the righteous endure in a corrupt society, the final word over their lives is well. This is not optimism but eschatological certainty — and it is enough to make perseverance possible.

3.reflection: Chapter 3 is uncomfortable precisely because its diagnoses are recognisable across every generation: bad governance as divine judgment, normalised shamelessness, the powerful exploiting the poor, status-display substituting for character. The pastoral response is not despair but the posture of verses 10–11: keep trusting that it shall be well with the righteous, and keep doing good.

4.subtitle: The Branch of the LORD
4.intro: Overview. Chapter 4 is only six verses — a brief but essential shaft of light after the darkness of chapter 3. Without it, the reader might conclude that Isaiah's God is nothing but a judge. Embedded here is one of the earliest Messianic titles in the book: the Branch of the LORD. The movement is from desolation (v. 1) to beauty and glory (vv. 2–6), from stripping to clothing, from exposure to shelter. What judgment removes, grace restores — and more than restores.

sections.title: Desolation: The Context for Grace
sections.commentary:
Verse 1 connects directly to the closing verses of chapter 3, where the men of Jerusalem have fallen in battle. The image of seven women seeking one man is a picture of demographic collapse — a society so depleted by war that normal social structures have been torn apart. “Seven” carries the sense of completeness; this is not an exceptional case but a widespread condition.

It is important not to skip verse 1 on the way to verse 2. The grace of verse 2 is only felt when the desolation of verse 1 is held in full view. This is how God's comfort consistently works in Scripture: it comes into specific darkness, not over it. The branch grows from devastated ground.

sections.title: The Branch and the Cloud of Glory
sections.commentary:
“In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious.” The Branch (tsemach) is a Messianic title Isaiah introduces here and that later prophets develop richly — Jeremiah calls him “a righteous Branch” who will execute justice (Jer 23:5); Zechariah applies it to the coming king-priest who will build the temple of God (Zech 6:12–13). In Isaiah 4 the Branch appears in the aftermath of judgment as the one in whom beauty and glory are restored — a remarkable contrast with the Servant of chapter 53, who had “no form or majesty that we should look at him.” Both are true: the Branch comes first in hidden glory, then in open magnificence.

v. 3 — “He who is left in Zion… will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem.” The phrase recorded for life is election language. The survivor community is not one that escaped disaster by luck; it is one specifically preserved and specifically cleansed (v. 4). This anticipates the New Testament doctrine of a people chosen by God and kept through every storm.

The closing image of cloud by day and fire by night is explicitly new-exodus language — the divine presence that guided Israel through the wilderness now covering the entire redeemed community. God's presence, once mediated through a portable tent, will shelter the whole people. Revelation 21:3 announces its final form: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.”

keyVerse.quote: “In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: The title “Branch” introduced here is one of the richest Messianic descriptions in the Old Testament. It suggests organic growth — something that grows naturally from existing roots rather than arriving as an alien intrusion. Jesus is not an afterthought to Israel's story; he grows from it, as a branch from a tree. And in him, what was laid waste becomes beautiful again.

4.theology:
The Messianic Branch. Isaiah 4:2 introduces a title that runs through the prophets and reaches its fulfilment in Christ. The Branch theology emphasises continuity (he grows from the root of Israel's history, from the line of David) and transformation (he brings what the tree itself could never produce — holiness, glory, shelter for all who come to him). Matthew's genealogy matters because Jesus is the Branch, traceable to Abraham and David.

Remnant and election. The concept of the preserved remnant — those “recorded for life” — runs throughout Isaiah. It is not earned survival but sovereign preservation. Paul develops this in Romans 9–11: the existence of a faithful remnant within Israel is always a demonstration of grace, never of deserving.
4.reflection: Chapter 4 is the antidote to despair after the severity of chapters 1–3. Judgment is real; the stripping is real. But the Branch of the LORD is also real — and he is coming. The community that will receive him is not the proudest or most impressive, but the survivors: those who have been through the fire and found that God was in it.

5.subtitle: The Song of the Vineyard and the Six Woes
5.intro: Overview. Chapter 5 is one of Isaiah's most accomplished literary compositions. It opens with a love song that turns into a lawsuit (vv. 1–7), catalogues six specific moral and social sins with the prophetic “Woe” associated with funeral laments (vv. 8–23), and closes with a vision of judgment so swift it leaves no room for delay (vv. 24–30). Jesus knew this chapter intimately; his parable of the tenants in Matthew 21 is a direct retelling of the vineyard song, using the same rhetorical strategy of drawing hearers into passing judgment before they realise they are the ones in the dock.

sections.title: The Song of the Vineyard
sections.commentary:
Isaiah opens as a singer performing a love song about his friend's vineyard. Listeners expect a celebration. As they hear of all the careful preparation — the choice hillside, the clearing of stones, the planted vines, the watchtower, the wine vat — they are drawn into sympathy with the farmer. Then the twist: after all that investment, wild grapes. The farmer invites the audience to judge: “What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it?” Nothing. The failure is entirely the vineyard's. Before the listeners realise it, they have judged themselves.

v. 7 — “He looked for justice (mishpat), but behold, bloodshed (mispach); for righteousness (tsedaqah), but behold, an outcry (tse'aqah).” Isaiah's Hebrew puns are untranslatable but unforgettable. The vineyard produced the exact inverse of what it was planted to yield — not ignorance of God's standard but systematic inversion of it.

sections.title: The Six Woes
sections.commentary:
The six woes cover the sins that most thoroughly unravel a society. The first (v. 8) targets covetous land accumulation — the wealthy systematically displacing small landowners until entire communities are dispossessed. The second (vv. 11–12) targets hedonism without God: feasting, music, and wine consumed as ends in themselves, so that the revellers “do not regard the deeds of the LORD.” It is possible to be surrounded by beauty and culture and remain entirely blind to God.

The fourth woe (v. 20) speaks most directly across every age: Woe to those who call evil good and good evil. This is not simple moral confusion but moral inversion — a systematic relabelling of God's categories. Sproul often observed that the greatest danger to a society is not that it does evil but that it redefines evil as good, thereby removing any vocabulary for repentance. When darkness is called light, people stop looking for the switch.

v. 21 — “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight!” Intellectual pride — the refusal to submit one's judgments to the word of God — is the root from which moral inversion grows. The order of the woes is not accidental: self-wisdom precedes and enables the inversion of moral categories.

sections.title: The Coming Judgment
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends with the sound of an army. The force described in verses 26–29 is terrifyingly efficient: no one tired, no one stumbling, not a sandal strap broken, arrows sharp, bows bent. God does not improvise; he whistles, and they come.

v. 25 — “For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.” This phrase becomes a haunting refrain in chapters 9–10, repeated four times. Each repetition marks another stage of judgment on a people who will not turn back. God's patience is purposeful — and it has a limit.

The chapter closes in darkness — the answer to the unanswered question of verse 4: “What more was there to do?” When every care has been given and the vineyard still produces wild grapes, what remains is night. But Isaiah's book does not end here. The same voice that pronounces this darkness will say in 9:2: “the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.”

keyVerse.quote: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!”
keyVerse.note: This woe does not describe a society that has forgotten God's standards but one that has actively inverted them. The triple parallelism (evil/good, darkness/light, bitter/sweet) emphasises that this is comprehensive and deliberate. Once a culture reaches this stage, self-correction from within is almost impossible — the moral vocabulary needed for repentance has been destroyed. Only a word from outside the system can break through.

5.theology: Covenant and social justice. The woes of Isaiah 5 are not primarily political commentary; they are covenant charges. Israel was called to be a society that embodied God's character — justice for the poor, honest weights, truthful speech. The woes describe what a covenant community looks like when it has abandoned the God of the covenant while keeping its religious forms. Social justice in Isaiah is always the fruit of true worship, never its substitute.
5.reflection: Isaiah 5 asks the question God himself asks of the vineyard: what more could have been done? Everything was provided; nothing more could be given. The chapter is an invitation to honest self-examination — not only about the sins of society, but about the fruit one's own life is bearing for the One who planted it with such care.
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. <sup>2</sup>He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. <sup>3</sup>And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. <sup>4</sup>What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? <sup>12</sup>They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands. <sup>13</sup>Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst. <sup>14</sup>Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and the nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down, her revelers and he who exults in her. <sup>15</sup>Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low. <sup>16</sup>But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy in righteousness. <sup>17</sup>Then the lambs shall graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich. <sup>18</sup>Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes, <sup>19</sup>who say: "Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!" <sup>20</sup>Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter! <sup>21</sup>Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight! <sup>22</sup>Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink, <sup>23</sup>who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right! <sup>24</sup>Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. <sup>25</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains quaked; and their corpses were as refuse in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. <sup>26</sup>He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come! <sup>27</sup>None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken; <sup>28</sup>their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind. <sup>29</sup>Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue. <sup>30</sup>They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds.

50.subtitle: The Servant’s Obedience
50.intro: Overview. Chapter 50 contains the third Servant Song (vv. 4–9), one of four passages in Isaiah 40–55 where an unnamed figure — identified by the New Testament as Jesus — speaks in the first person about his calling and suffering. The Song is framed by two passages that give it context: God’s unanswered questions about Israel’s unfaithfulness (vv. 1–3), and a closing challenge about two ways of responding to darkness (vv. 10–11). What emerges is a portrait of the Servant as the one who models everything Israel failed to be — attentive where she was deaf, obedient where she was rebellious, trusting where she was self-reliant.

sections.title: The LORD’s Unanswered Questions
sections.commentary:
God opens the chapter with two rhetorical questions addressed to the exiles: Where is the divorce certificate that proves I sent Israel away? Who is the creditor to whom I sold you? The expected answer to both is: there is none. God did not issue a divorce; Israel walked out. He sold no one; the people sold themselves through their own sins. The point is carefully chosen. A divorced wife has been formally and permanently sent away. A sold slave can still be redeemed. By framing the exile in terms of debt rather than divorce, God is already hinting that the door back is open.

Verses 2–3 reverse the direction: it was not God who was absent, but the people. He came and called; no one answered. This failure of response — God speaking, Israel not listening — is one of the defining patterns of Isaiah. It makes the Servant’s posture in the next section all the more striking. Where the nation turned a deaf ear, the Servant wakes each morning to listen.

v. 2 — “Why, when I came, was there no one? When I called, was there no one to answer?” The same lament echoes at the end of the book (65:12; 66:4). The tragedy is not divine absence but human unresponsiveness. The one who made the sea and dried it up was more than capable of acting; what he found was a people who had stopped listening.

sections.title: The Third Servant Song — Morning by Morning
sections.commentary:
The Servant speaks. His opening self-description is not of power or authority but of being taught. God has given him the tongue of those who are taught — a disciple’s tongue — so that he knows how to speak a sustaining word to the weary. Before the Servant can minister to the exhausted, he must first receive. Before he speaks, he listens. This pattern — formation before deployment, reception before proclamation — runs against every instinct toward self-sufficiency.

v. 4 — “Morning by morning he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” The repetition of morning by morning is deliberate: the daily discipline of attentiveness is what produces the tongue that can sustain the weary. R.C. Sproul noted that the great preachers are always, first, the great listeners.

Verses 5–6 move from formation to suffering. The Servant did not rebel, did not turn back — and was beaten, had his beard pulled, was spat on. The specificity should stop the reader: Isaiah is not describing symbolic suffering but physical particulars that Matthew 26:67 and 27:30 record as history. The Gospel writers noted these details as events; Isaiah named them as prophecy seven centuries earlier.

The section closes with confidence: “The Lord GOD helps me — therefore I have set my face like a flint.” Luke 9:51 uses this exact language of Jesus turning toward Jerusalem. The courtroom image of verses 8–9 becomes in Paul’s hands the cry of Romans 8:33: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?”

sections.title: Two Ways of Walking in Darkness
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends by placing two kinds of people before two different futures. The first fears the LORD, obeys the Servant’s voice, and yet walks in darkness — no light, no felt assurance, no visible sign that trust is warranted. To this person God gives a single instruction: trust, and rely on your God. The second person lights their own fire, surrounding themselves with their own sparks — the refusal to wait on God producing its own alternative. The verdict is blunt: you shall lie down in torment. The fires kindled for comfort become the fire they inhabit.

v. 10 — “Let him trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God.” This is the practical application of everything the Servant demonstrated. He walked toward suffering with his face set like flint — not because he could see the outcome, but because he knew who held it. The same confidence is now extended to all who follow in his way.

keyVerse.quote: “But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.”
keyVerse.note: The confidence here is entirely derivative — it flows from God’s help, not the Servant’s constitution. Luke 9:51 applies “set his face” directly to Jesus heading to Jerusalem, and the deliberateness is the point: he is not swept toward the cross by events but walks toward it with resolution, grounded in the certainty that the Father is with him.

50.reflection: The Servant’s day begins with listening before speaking, receiving before giving. This is not merely a spiritual discipline — it is the source of the sustaining word he is able to offer the weary. Where are you most tempted to speak, teach, or act before you have first sat quietly to receive? And where in your life are you lighting your own fire rather than waiting in the dark for God’s?
50.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. <sup>2</sup>Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst. <sup>3</sup>I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering." <sup>4</sup>The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. <sup>5</sup>The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. <sup>6</sup>I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting. <sup>7</sup>But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame. <sup>8</sup>He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. <sup>9</sup>Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up. <sup>10</sup>Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God. <sup>11</sup>Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment.

51.subtitle: Look to the Rock from Which You Were Cut
51.intro: Overview. Chapter 51 is a sustained call to remembrance — look back to Abraham, look back to the exodus, look up to the heavens God made — as the ground for present courage. God’s salvation will last when the heavens vanish; his righteousness endures forever. The chapter ends with the cup of wrath taken from Israel’s lips and placed in the hand of her oppressors.

sections.title: Look to Abraham
sections.commentary:
Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were cut, to the quarry from which you were hewn. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you — when he was but one I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. One man, childless, and from him came a nation. The logic of the call is: if God can do that from one, he can rebuild Zion from its ruins.

v. 6 — “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.” The contrast is between two kinds of permanence. The heavens and earth feel maximally stable — but they are contingent and will pass. God’s salvation is not contingent; it will outlast the cosmos. 2 Pet. 3:10–13 and Rev. 21:1 describe this passing from the outside.

sections.title: The Arm of the LORD
sections.commentary:
Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in the days of old. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who dried up the sea, who made the depths into a road for the redeemed? The appeal to the exodus is not nostalgia but argument: the same arm that acted then can act now.

God promises to comfort Zion and silence the one who taunts. Then the reversal: the cup of staggering — the bowl of God’s wrath that Jerusalem has been drinking — will be taken from her hand and placed in the hand of those who afflicted her. The suffering is not permanent; the oppressors’ temporary power is not the final arrangement.

keyVerse.quote: “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.”
keyVerse.note: The permanence of God’s salvation is grounded in the impermanence of everything else. When even the heavens and earth are revealed as contingent, the one thing that stands is what God has declared. This is not escapism but realism: the most stable-seeming things will pass; the apparently fragile promise will not.

51.reflection: God says: look to Abraham — I called one man and multiplied him. Where in your situation does the evidence look like “only one” or “only remnant”? What would it mean to draw courage from the Abraham-logic: that God specializes in beginnings that look statistically impossible?
51.text: <sup>1</sup>"Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the quarry from which you were dug. <sup>2</sup>Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you; for he was but one when I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. <sup>3</sup>For the LORD comforts Zion; he comforts all her waste places and makes her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of song. <sup>4</sup>Give attention to me, my people, and give ear to me, my nation; for a law will go out from me, and I will set my justice for a light to the peoples. <sup>5</sup>My righteousness draws near, my salvation has gone out, and my arms will judge the peoples; the coastlands hope for me, and for my arm they wait. <sup>6</sup>Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and they who dwell in it will die in like manner; but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed. <sup>7</sup>Listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man, nor be dismayed at their revilings. <sup>8</sup>For the moth will eat them up like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool, but my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to all generations." <sup>9</sup>Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in days of old, the generations of long ago.
