52.subtitle: How Beautiful Are the Feet
52.intro: Overview. Chapter 52 is a trumpet call to Zion — wake up, get up, shake off the dust, put on your beautiful garments. The exile is ending; the prisoners are being released; the herald is coming. The famous verse about beautiful feet brings the good news of peace, salvation, and the reign of God. The chapter ends with the introduction to the greatest of the Servant Songs: “Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up.”

sections.title: Awake, O Zion
sections.commentary:
Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem. Shake yourself free of the dust; arise, O captive Jerusalem. For the LORD has redeemed Jerusalem. The grounds for the command are the indicative of redemption: the imperative to rise is grounded in the fact of being ransomed.

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns.” Paul quotes verse 7 twice (Rom. 10:15; Eph. 6:15) as the description of gospel proclamation. The content of the good news is compressed into three phrases: peace, happiness (welfare), salvation. And the summary: your God reigns. The whole mission of the herald is to announce that God has taken up his kingship.

v. 7 — “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’” The beauty falls on the feet — the most pedestrian part of the body — because it is the one who comes that matters. The message is not beautiful because of how it is packaged but because of what it announces: the end of exile and the beginning of God’s reign.

sections.title: The Servant Introduced
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with the opening lines of the fourth Servant Song: Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted. As many were astonished at him — his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance — so he shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths. The exaltation and the disfigurement belong together. The one who is highest was lowest; the one who astonishes kings was astonishing in his suffering first.

keyVerse.quote: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace… who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’”
keyVerse.note: Paul’s use of this verse in Romans 10:15 extends the herald imagery to every Christian witness. The feet are beautiful not because the herald is but because of what they carry. Every announcement of the gospel is an echo of this verse: “your God reigns” is the irreducible content of Christian proclamation.

52.reflection: Zion is told to shake off the dust and put on beautiful garments — before she sees the full deliverance. The command to rise precedes the visible evidence that rising makes sense. Where in your life is God calling you to rise and dress for freedom before you can yet see the liberation he has promised?
52.text: <sup>1</sup>Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on your beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean. <sup>2</sup>Shake yourself from the dust and arise; be seated, O Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, O captive daughter of Zion. <sup>3</sup>For thus says the LORD: "You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money." <sup>4</sup>For thus says the Lord GOD: "My people went down at the first into Egypt to sojourn there, and the Assyrian oppressed them for nothing. <sup>5</sup>Now therefore what have I here," declares the LORD, "seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail," declares the LORD, "and continually all the day my name is despised. <sup>6</sup>Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore in that day they shall know that it is I who speak; here I am." <sup>7</sup>How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, "Your God reigns." <sup>8</sup>The voice of your watchmen— they lift up their voice; together they sing for joy; for eye to eye they see the return of the LORD to Zion. <sup>9</sup>Break forth together into singing, you waste places of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. <sup>10</sup>The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. <sup>11</sup>Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. <sup>12</sup>For you shall not go out in haste, and you shall not go in flight, for the LORD will go before you, and the God of Israel will be your rear guard. <sup>13</sup>Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted. <sup>14</sup>As many were astonished at you— his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance, and his form beyond that of the children of mankind— <sup>15</sup>so shall he sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him; for that which has not been told them they see, and that which they have not heard they understand.

53.subtitle: The Suffering Servant
53.intro: Overview. Isaiah 53 is the summit of the book and one of the most theologically dense passages in all of Scripture. The fourth Servant Song (52:13–53:12) describes a figure who suffers not for his own sin but for the sins of others — pierced for transgressions, crushed for iniquities, bearing the iniquity of us all. The New Testament identifies the Servant as Jesus Christ, and more of Isaiah 53 is quoted in the New Testament than any other Old Testament passage. The text is written in the past tense, as if the suffering is already accomplished and the speakers are looking back in astonished confession.

sections.title: Who Has Believed Our Report?
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a question that is also a lament: who has believed what he heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? The Servant grew up like a young plant, like a root out of dry ground. He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief — and we hid our faces from him; we esteemed him not.

The confession is extraordinary: we did not see what we were looking at. The arm of the LORD was at work in the one we turned away from. John quotes verse 1 at the end of his account of Jesus’ public ministry (John 12:38) as the explanation for why the crowds did not believe despite the signs. The message was there; the believing was not.

sections.title: Pierced for Our Transgressions
sections.commentary:
The center of the chapter — and perhaps the center of the entire Old Testament. He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.

The substitutionary logic is precise: our transgressions, our iniquities, our peace, our healing — but the piercing and crushing fall on him. Peter quotes verse 24 directly in 1 Pet. 2:24: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.” Paul’s entire theology of the atonement traces back to this passage.

v. 6 — “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned — every one — to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” The universality of the straying (“all we”; “every one”) meets the singularity of the bearing (“on him”). The LORD is the agent: he is the one who lays the iniquity. This is not the Servant volunteering for something God did not plan; it is God’s own act of transferring the weight.

sections.title: He Was Silent
sections.commentary:
He was oppressed and afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb led to slaughter, like a sheep before its shearers, he was silent. By oppression and judgment he was taken away. Who considered that he was cut off from the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? They made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death — a detail Matthew records precisely (27:57–60): buried in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea.

The silence is not passive; it is chosen. The Servant of chapter 50 set his face like flint and gave himself voluntarily. The silence before accusers is the same agency as the set face — the Servant is not a victim of the proceedings but the one directing them from within.

sections.title: He Shall See and Be Satisfied
sections.commentary:
Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief. When his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.

v. 11 — “Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied.” This is justification language: the Servant sees the result of his suffering — the many made righteous — and is satisfied. The satisfaction is God’s justice met and the Servant’s joy complete. It is the theological ground of Hebrews 12:2: “for the joy set before him he endured the cross.”

Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors. The chapter ends with the Servant alive, interceding, victorious — resurrection implied in every word.

keyVerse.quote: “But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed.”
keyVerse.note: This verse is the clearest statement of penal substitutionary atonement in the entire Bible. The prepositions carry the weight: for our transgressions, for our iniquities. The chastisement (divine judicial punishment) fell on him so that peace could come to us. This is not one theory of the atonement among others — it is the grammar Isaiah uses to describe what God planned.

53.theology: Penal Substitutionary Atonement. Isaiah 53 is the Old Testament’s fullest statement of what the New Testament calls penal substitution: the righteous one bearing the punishment that belonged to the unrighteous. The key elements are all present — the guilt of “all we” (v. 6), the transfer by God himself (“the LORD has laid on him”), the specific categories of piercing for transgressions and crushing for iniquities (v. 5), and the result: peace and healing for those whose iniquity he bore. Reformed theology has consistently held that this is not merely one way of describing the atonement but its structural core — the mechanism by which the justice of God and the mercy of God are both fully expressed in a single act at Calvary. R.C. Sproul called Isaiah 53 the chapter that makes the cross comprehensible.
53.reflection: The chapter opens with a question about believing: “Who has believed what he heard from us?” And it closes with intercession: the Servant makes intercession for the transgressors. You are among the transgressors for whom he intercedes. What difference does it make — practically, emotionally, theologically — to know that the risen Christ is right now interceding for you at the Father’s right hand (Rom. 8:34)?
53.text: <sup>1</sup>Who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? <sup>2</sup>For he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground; he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. <sup>3</sup>He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. <sup>4</sup>Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. <sup>5</sup>But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed. <sup>6</sup>All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned— every one— to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. <sup>7</sup>He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. <sup>8</sup>By oppression and judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people? <sup>9</sup>And they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. <sup>10</sup>Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. <sup>11</sup>Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. <sup>12</sup>Therefore I will divide him a portion with the many, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.

6.subtitle: Holy, Holy, Holy — Isaiah's Vision and Call
6.intro: Overview. Chapter 6 is one of the most significant passages in the entire Bible. Isaiah receives a vision of the LORD enthroned in his heavenly temple, surrounded by seraphim who cry the trisagion — “Holy, holy, holy.” The vision undoes him completely; he confesses his uncleanness and is cleansed by a coal from the altar. Then he hears the divine council deliberating and responds with the most famous volunteer in Scripture: “Here am I! Send me.” The commission he is given is deeply strange — he is told to speak words that will harden rather than soften, until the land is devastated. Yet even here, a holy seed remains in the stump.

sections.title: The Vision of the Holy God
sections.commentary:
The vision is anchored in history: “In the year that King Uzziah died.” Uzziah had reigned for fifty-two years — an entire generation of stability. His death was a political crisis. Isaiah receives this vision precisely when human leadership has failed, and what he sees is not a successor king but the King who never vacates his throne. The LORD is “high and lifted up” — the same Hebrew phrase used in 52:13 of the Servant. The temple is full of his train: not his robe but the overflow of his glory, so vast that its hem fills the entire sanctuary.

The seraphim — literally “burning ones” — cover their faces and their feet in the presence of God. They have been in his presence continually; they have never grown used to it. Their worship is not performance but prostration. And what they cry is not “powerful, powerful, powerful” or “glorious, glorious, glorious” but “holy, holy, holy.” Holiness is the attribute of attributes — the one quality of God that receives the threefold emphasis.

v. 3 — “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.” The trisagion — used again in Revelation 4:8 — is the highest form of emphasis available in Hebrew. Not just holy, not doubly holy, but holy beyond all comparison. The holiness proclaimed here is not merely moral purity but ontological otherness: God is categorically unlike anything in creation.

sections.title: Woe Is Me — The Coal from the Altar
sections.commentary:
Isaiah's response to the vision is not “how wonderful” but “woe is me.” He does not say “I am not worthy”; he says “I am undone” — the word means to be destroyed, to come apart. His first concern is the specific failure of his lips: “I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips.” He has just heard lips burning with perfect praise; his own lips have never come close. The comparison is annihilating.

v. 5 — “For my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!” Isaiah does not say he has seen God's back or his shadow. He has seen the King. John 12:41 identifies this vision as a sight of Christ's glory: “Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.” The vision of Isaiah 6 is, in John's reading, a vision of the pre-incarnate Son.

The seraph's response is immediate: a coal from the altar — the place of sacrifice — touched to the lips. “Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.” The cleansing does not come from Isaiah's efforts; it comes from the altar. Atonement is the answer to the problem that holiness exposes. What the vision breaks, the sacrifice repairs.

sections.title: The Call, the Commission, and the Strange Message
sections.commentary:
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” The plural “us” in a divine context has long been read by Christian interpreters as a trace of the trinitarian life — a deliberation within the Godhead. Isaiah's response — “Here am I! Send me” — is not presumption but the overflow of a man who has been cleansed. He could not have said it in verse 5; he can say it in verse 8 because the coal has done its work. Readiness for service follows from, and does not precede, the experience of grace.

The commission is difficult. Isaiah is told to speak so that the people will hear without understanding and see without perceiving, their hearts growing fat and their ears heavy. This is judicial hardening — a sovereign act in which continued rejection of the word results in increasing incapacity to receive it. Jesus quotes this passage in Matthew 13:14–15 to explain his parables. Paul cites it in Acts 28:26–27 to explain Israel's unbelief. The hardening is real, it is just, and it is the consequence of prior rejection.

v. 13 — “The holy seed is its stump.” The chapter ends not in total darkness but with a remnant image. A felled tree still has a stump, and a stump can still produce a shoot. This seed anticipates the Branch of chapter 4, the root of Jesse in chapter 11, and ultimately the one who grows from apparently barren ground in chapter 53.

keyVerse.quote: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”
keyVerse.note: The trisagion is the heart of Isaiah's vision and arguably the heart of the entire book. Every chapter of Isaiah flows from this reality: God is holy, and the earth belongs to him. Judgment is what holiness does when it encounters persistent unrepentance. Comfort is what holiness does when it encounters the broken and contrite. The missionary call of verse 8 is also a response to this: if the whole earth is full of his glory, the whole earth needs to hear about it.

6.theology:
The holiness of God. Isaiah 6 is the definitive Old Testament text on holiness as God's fundamental attribute. Holiness is not primarily about moral purity (though it includes it) but about God's absolute separateness from everything created. He is the only self-existent being; everything else derives its existence from him. This is why the seraphim cover themselves: in the presence of uncreated holiness, the most exalted of created beings are utterly undone.

Atonement and access. The movement of verses 5–7 is the movement of the entire gospel: the vision of holiness produces awareness of guilt; guilt produces the cry of undoing; and in response to that cry, God provides cleansing from the altar. Isaiah does not clean himself up before approaching God; God reaches to him. Access to the holy God is always the result of atonement, never of moral self-improvement.

The Trinity. The plural “us” of verse 8, combined with John 12:41 (identifying the vision as a sight of Christ) and the Spirit's role throughout the prophets, has led the church from its earliest centuries to read Isaiah 6 as a scene in which all three persons are present.
6.reflection: Isaiah's “Here am I! Send me” is often quoted as a model of eagerness for service — but it only makes sense after what precedes it. He is not a volunteer who has assessed the risks and decided to help. He is a ruined man who has been remade by the coal from the altar, and his readiness is the overflow of that experience. True willingness for costly service is always downstream of being undone and restored.
6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. <sup>2</sup>Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew. <sup>3</sup>And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" <sup>4</sup>And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. <sup>5</sup>And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!" <sup>6</sup>Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having in his hand a burning coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar. <sup>7</sup>And he touched my mouth and said: "Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for." <sup>8</sup>And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am! Send me." <sup>9</sup>And he said, "Go, and say to this people: 'Keep on hearing, but do not understand; keep on seeing, but do not perceive.' <sup>10</sup>Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed." <sup>11</sup>Then I said, "How long, O Lord?" And he said: "Until cities lie waste without inhabitant, and houses without people, and the land is a desolate waste, <sup>12</sup>and the LORD removes people far away, and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land. <sup>13</sup>And though a tenth remain in it, it will be burned again, like a terebinth or an oak, whose stump remains when it is felled." The holy seed is its stump.

7.subtitle: The Sign of Immanuel
7.intro: Overview. Chapter 7 is set during the Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 734–732 BC), when the kingdoms of Syria and northern Israel formed an alliance against Judah. King Ahaz of Jerusalem, faced with this threat, is leaning toward appealing to Assyria rather than trusting God. Isaiah is sent with a message of reassurance — and with a call to faith that Ahaz refuses. The sign God offers in response to that refusal is one of the most contested and theologically significant prophecies in the Old Testament: a young woman will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel. Matthew 1:23 identifies the ultimate fulfilment of this sign as the virgin birth of Jesus.

sections.title: Fear Not — Stand Firm in Faith
sections.commentary:
The political situation is desperate. The armies of Syria and Ephraim are marching toward Jerusalem, and “the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (v. 2). Isaiah is sent with his son Shear-jashub — whose name means “a remnant shall return” — to meet the king at the Fuller's Field. The child's presence is itself a message: even if judgment comes, a remnant will remain.

God's assessment of the threat is deliberately deflating: Syria and Ephraim are “two smoldering stumps of firebrands” (v. 4). They were once dangerous fires; now they are dying embers. The scheme to replace Ahaz with a puppet king will not succeed. Isaiah's word is categorical: “It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass.”

v. 9 — “If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.” The Hebrew is a wordplay on the root aman (to be firm, to trust — the root of “amen”). The stability of Ahaz's kingdom depends not on Assyrian military aid but on whether his faith rests on the word of God. Trust is not a religious extra but the basis of all true security.

sections.title: The Sign of Immanuel
sections.commentary:
God offers Ahaz a sign — anything, from the depths to the heights of heaven. Ahaz refuses, cloaking his unbelief in the language of piety: “I will not put the LORD to the test.” Isaiah's response is one of the most exasperated sentences in all the prophets: “Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?” Ahaz is not being devout; he is hiding. He has already decided to trust Assyria, and a sign from God would complicate that decision.

v. 14 — “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.” The Hebrew word almah means a young woman of marriageable age — always a virgin in its Old Testament usage. The Greek Septuagint translates it with parthenos, the unambiguous word for virgin, and Matthew 1:23 quotes the LXX in applying the verse to Jesus. A near fulfilment existed in Isaiah's day; the ultimate fulfilment — the one the near event pointed toward — is the birth of Christ.

The name “Immanuel” — God with us — is the theological centre of the sign. God is not dealing with his people from a safe distance. He will enter their situation personally. This is what the incarnation fulfils in a way no near-term birth could: in Jesus, God is literally, bodily, materially with us.

sections.title: The Razor from Assyria
sections.commentary: The chapter closes with a series of oracles describing what the Assyrian alliance Ahaz has chosen will actually produce. God will whistle for Egypt and Assyria, and the very power Ahaz is relying on for deliverance will be the instrument of devastation. The image of the hired razor shaving everything off — head, beard, legs — is one of profound humiliation. Ahaz thought he was hiring Assyria; Isaiah tells him God is hiring Assyria — and the target is not just the enemies but Judah itself. Faith deferred always costs more than the thing it was trying to avoid.

keyVerse.quote: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”
keyVerse.note: The sign is given not to Ahaz but despite Ahaz — it is addressed to “the house of David” (v. 13), the dynasty that will eventually produce the one the sign points to. Matthew's use of this verse is not an imposition on the text but the fulfilment of what the near event was designed to foreshadow: a birth that is genuinely miraculous, a child who is genuinely God-with-us, in a way that no ordinary birth in Isaiah's day could be.

7.theology:
Dual fulfilment of prophecy. Isaiah 7:14 is the clearest example in Scripture of a prophecy with both a near and an ultimate fulfilment. The near sign existed in Isaiah's own day; the ultimate sign is the birth of Christ. Prophecy in this model is like a shadow cast by an object in front of a light — the shadow tells you something real about the shape of the object, but the object is greater than the shadow.

The incarnation as answer to fear. The context of Isaiah 7 is terror — a shaking king, a threatened city. God's response is not a battle plan but a name: Immanuel. The answer to human fear in the face of overwhelming circumstances is always the same in Scripture: God with us. This is what the incarnation means in Matthew 1 — not a new religious idea but the arrival, in person, of the one Isaiah promised to the frightened house of David.
7.reflection: Ahaz's refusal of a sign is a portrait of a peculiarly religious form of unbelief: using the language of reverence to avoid the demand of trust. It is possible to be scrupulously religious while refusing to actually rely on God. The question Isaiah's chapter asks is the same one it asked Ahaz: where is your security actually resting — on the word of God, or on the alliance you have quietly arranged?
7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah the king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but could not yet mount an attack against it. <sup>2</sup>When the house of David was told, "Syria is in league with Ephraim," the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind. <sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Isaiah, "Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. <sup>4</sup>And say to him, 'Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria and the son of Remaliah. <sup>5</sup>Because Syria, with Ephraim and the son of Remaliah, has devised evil against you, saying, <sup>6</sup>"Let us go up against Judah and terrify it, and let us conquer it for ourselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in the midst of it," <sup>7</sup>thus says the Lord GOD: It shall not stand, and it shall not come to pass. <sup>8</sup>For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered from being a people. <sup>9</sup>And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all.'" <sup>10</sup>Again the LORD spoke to Ahaz: <sup>11</sup>"Ask a sign of the LORD your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven." <sup>12</sup>But Ahaz said, "I will not ask, and I will not put the LORD to the test." <sup>13</sup>And he said, "Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also? <sup>14</sup>Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. <sup>15</sup>He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good. <sup>16</sup>For before the boy knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread will be deserted. <sup>17</sup>The LORD will bring upon you and upon your people and upon your father's house such days as have not come since the day that Ephraim departed from Judah— the king of Assyria." <sup>18</sup>In that day the LORD will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the streams of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria. <sup>19</sup>And they will all come and settle in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and on all the thornbushes, and on all the pastures. <sup>20</sup>In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River— with the king of Assyria— the head and the hair of the feet, and it will sweep away the beard also. <sup>21</sup>In that day a man will keep alive a young cow and two sheep, <sup>22</sup>and because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey. <sup>23</sup>In that day every place where there used to be a thousand vines, worth a thousand shekels of silver, will become briers and thorns. <sup>24</sup>With bow and arrows a man will come there, for all the land will be briers and thorns. <sup>25</sup>And as for all the hills that used to be hoed with a hoe, you will not come there for fear of briers and thorns, but they will become a place where cattle are let loose and where sheep tread.

8.subtitle: Fear God Alone
8.intro: Overview. Chapter 8 continues directly from chapter 7, moving through the immediate fulfilment of the Immanuel sign in the birth of Isaiah's second son, to the announcement that Assyria will overwhelm the land like a flood, to a searching call to fear God rather than the conspiracies and crises that are making everyone else afraid. The chapter ends in darkness — those who have rejected the word of God have no light — but Isaiah and his children stand within that darkness as living signs of God's purposes.

sections.title: Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz and the Flood of Assyria
sections.commentary:
Isaiah's second son is given a name that means “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil” — a prophecy in a name. Before the child is old enough to say “my father” or “my mother,” the wealth of Damascus and Samaria will be carried off by Assyria. The sign is specific and dated: this is not vague prophecy but a named child whose growth will mark the timeline of fulfilment.

The image of the waters of Shiloah (v. 6) — the gentle stream through Jerusalem — being rejected in favour of the mighty Euphrates is one of Isaiah's most powerful metaphors. Judah has despised the quiet provision of God and longed for the impressive power of Assyria. The consequence is that the great river will come — but it will not stop at the border. It will rise “up to the neck,” leaving only the head above water. The very power chosen as a solution becomes the flooding problem.

v. 10 — “Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us.” The chapter places Immanuel here as a battle cry — not just a name but a declaration that all the plotting of the nations runs up against the fact of God's presence. Every alliance that does not account for God is building on nothing.

sections.title: Fear the LORD of Hosts
sections.commentary:
The LORD speaks directly to Isaiah and calls him out of the prevailing culture of fear: “Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread.” The nation is in a panic over Syria and Ephraim. God's word to Isaiah is: their fear is misplaced. Calibrate your dread to the right object.

v. 13 — “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honour as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” Fear of God is not offered here as a competitor to wisdom or courage but as their source. The person who fears God properly will not be paralysed by the fear of circumstances, because they understand that the one who controls all circumstances is also the one who is for them. Peter quotes this verse in 1 Peter 3:14–15, applying it to Christians facing persecution.

The closing verses are stark. Those who do not speak according to the law and testimony — the word of God — have no light in them. In the darkness that follows the rejection of God's word, people will look to the dead and find no answer. Isaiah and his children stand as signs and portents — living testimonies that God has spoken, even when the word is not welcomed.

keyVerse.quote: “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honour as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.”
keyVerse.note: This verse reorients what fear is for. Fear is not to be eliminated but redirected. The person who fears the right thing — the LORD of hosts — will be freed from the paralysing fear of everything else. Peter's use of this text in 1 Peter 3 makes the application explicit: in a hostile world, the answer to anxiety about circumstances is not stoic courage but a heart that is occupied with the holiness of God.

8.reflection: The chapter diagnoses a failure that is both common and hard to see in oneself: calibrating one's fear to the wrong object. The people of Judah were afraid of the right threats by the wrong standard — afraid of Syria when they should have been afraid of the God who governs Syria. The question the chapter asks directly: what is it in your own situation that is producing your deepest anxiety, and is that fear proportioned to the reality of who God is?
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to me, "Take a large tablet and write on it in common characters, 'Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.'" <sup>2</sup>And I will get reliable witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah, to attest for me. <sup>3</sup>And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the LORD said to me, "Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz; <sup>4</sup>for before the boy knows how to cry 'My father' or 'My mother,' the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria." <sup>5</sup>The LORD spoke to me again: <sup>6</sup>"Because this people has refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently, and rejoice over Rezin and the son of Remaliah, <sup>7</sup>therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory. And it will rise over all its channels and go over all its banks, <sup>8</sup>and it will sweep on into Judah, it will overflow and pass on, reaching even to the neck, and its outspread wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Immanuel." <sup>9</sup>Be broken, you peoples, and be shattered; give ear, all you far countries; strap on your armor and be shattered; strap on your armor and be shattered. <sup>10</sup>Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us. <sup>11</sup>For the LORD spoke thus to me with his strong hand upon me, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying: <sup>12</sup>"Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. <sup>13</sup>But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. <sup>14</sup>And he will become a sanctuary and a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, a trap and a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. <sup>15</sup>And many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken; they shall be snared and taken." <sup>16</sup>Bind up the testimony; seal the teaching among my disciples. <sup>17</sup>I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and I will hope in him. <sup>18</sup>Behold, I and the children whom the LORD has given me are signs and portents in Israel from the LORD of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion. <sup>19</sup>And when they say to you, "Inquire of the mediums and the necromancers who chirp and mutter," should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living? <sup>20</sup>To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn. <sup>21</sup>They will pass through the land, greatly distressed and hungry. And when they are hungry, they will be enraged and will speak contemptuously against their king and their God, and turn their faces upward. <sup>22</sup>And they will look to the earth, but behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish. And they will be thrust into thick darkness.

9.subtitle: A Great Light — The Child Born to Us
9.intro: Overview. Chapter 9 moves from the darkness at the end of chapter 8 to one of the most luminous promises in all of Scripture. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. What follows is simultaneously poetic, political, and theological: a child has been born, a son has been given, and the government will rest on his shoulders. The four names given to this child constitute the most compressed Christology in the Old Testament. Chapter 9 is the prophetic foundation for every proclamation that points beyond the manger to the throne.

sections.title: A Great Light in the Darkness
sections.commentary:
Isaiah begins by specifying the geography of the promise: Zebulun and Naphtali, the northern territories — the very regions most thoroughly overrun by Assyria. These were the first to fall and the last anyone would expect to be glorified. Yet it is precisely these “Galilee of the nations” regions that will first see the great light. Matthew 4:13–16 quotes this passage to explain why Jesus based his ministry in Capernaum and Galilee rather than Jerusalem — the light goes first to the most forgotten places.

v. 3 — “You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the plunder.” The images are harvest and victory — abundance and vindication arriving simultaneously. The joy is not muted or tentative; it is the full-throated celebration of people who had long lived under oppression and now find it lifted.

sections.title: For Unto Us a Child Is Born
sections.commentary:
“For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder.” The construction is deliberate: the child is born (humanity) but the son is given (the gift comes from above). Both the human birth and the divine sending are stated. And the government — all authority, all rule — rests on this single shoulder. This is not a constitutional monarchy; this is the absolute and righteous reign of the one to whom all authority belongs.

The four names are given as a compound title — a unified description of who this child is:

v. 6 — The four names. Wonderful Counsellor: not a counsellor who is wonderful but one whose counsel is itself a wonder, beyond ordinary human wisdom. Mighty God (El Gibbor): the second name is unambiguous — this child is called God. Not godlike, not divine in some reduced sense, but El. Everlasting Father: the eternal source and sustainer of his people's life. Prince of Peace: the one in whom all the shalom Isaiah has described as history's goal actually arrives.

Verse 7 closes with a promise as comprehensive as it is unconditional: “Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end.” This kingdom will not peak and decline. It will not be subject to the cycles of rise and fall that mark every human empire. The “zeal of the LORD of hosts” will perform it. The guarantee is not human faithfulness but divine zeal.

keyVerse.quote: “For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
keyVerse.note: The name Mighty God (El Gibbor) is the same phrase used of God himself in Isaiah 10:21. Isaiah is not hedging when he calls this coming child God; he is asserting it. The full weight of orthodox Christology — the genuine divinity of the Son — has its Old Testament foundation here. Matthew, Luke, and John each draw on Isaiah 9 in their portraits of Jesus.

9.theology:
The person of Christ. The four names of Isaiah 9:6 have been central to the church's reflection on who Jesus is since the earliest centuries. The name Mighty God grounds the assertions of John 1:1 and Philippians 2:6 — that Jesus is not merely a great teacher but God himself. The child who is born is simultaneously the Son who is given: the human birth and the divine mission are two aspects of a single event.

The Kingdom of God. “The government shall be upon his shoulder” points to the political dimension of Christ's lordship that is often underemphasised. Jesus does not merely save individual souls; he rules a kingdom. The “increase of his government” with “no end” describes an expansion already underway — every person who comes under the reign of the Prince of Peace is a new territory in which the kingdom advances.
9.reflection: Isaiah 9 was written to people living in the specific darkness of Assyrian occupation. The promise of a child born to them was addressed to their situation, not over it. Whatever darkness you are living in, the promise is the same: “the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.” The question is not whether the light has come — it has — but whether you are facing it.

In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the latter time he has made glorious the way of the sea, the land beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. <sup>2</sup>The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone. <sup>3</sup>You have multiplied the nation; you have increased its joy; they rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest, as they are glad when they divide the spoil. <sup>4</sup>For the yoke of his burden, and the staff for his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, you have broken as on the day of Midian. <sup>5</sup>For every boot of the tramping warrior in battle tumult and every garment rolled in blood will be burned as fuel for the fire. <sup>6</sup>For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. <sup>7</sup>Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. 10.subtitle: Woe to Unjust Laws — Assyria the Rod of God
10.intro: Overview. Chapter 10 operates on two levels simultaneously. The first is immediate and political: God will use Assyria as his instrument of judgment against Israel, but Assyria's own arrogance means it will then be judged in turn. The second level is theological and universal: how does God govern history through the free actions of wicked human agents? The chapter offers no evasion of this question. God is sovereign over the nations; the nations are morally responsible for their own actions; both are fully true.

sections.title: Woe to Unjust Legislators
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens by continuing the woes of chapter 5. Woe to those who write laws designed to deprive the poor of their rights and make widows and orphans their plunder. This is not random corruption but systemic oppression built into the structure of society — laws crafted to protect the powerful by exploiting the vulnerable.

v. 3 — “What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar?” The day of reckoning cannot be legislated away. The same legal skill used to construct unjust systems is entirely useless when the God who is not subject to human law arrives. Wealth and legal ingenuity have never yet survived a divine audit.

sections.title: Assyria: The Rod of God's Anger
sections.commentary:
“Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!” God calls Assyria his rod — his instrument. The world's most powerful empire is a staff in the hand of the LORD, directed against Israel to punish her for her sins. Assyria does not know this (v. 7: “But he does not so intend”); the Assyrian king acts out of pure imperial ambition. Yet God is sovereign over the outcome.

The boast of the Assyrian king in verses 8–11 is magnificent in its arrogance: my commanders are all kings; I have taken city after city; shall Jerusalem not fare the same as Samaria? What the king does not perceive is that he is not the one swinging the axe — he is the axe. Axes do not take credit for the work of the carpenter.

vv. 15–16 — “Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it?” The image deflates the imperial self-understanding in a single question. Human power, however impressive, is always instrumental — always in the hand of a larger power. Assyria's failure was not incompetence; it was the assumption that its success was self-generated.

Assyria's judgment is therefore just: not for doing what God used it to do, but for the pride and cruelty with which it did it. God holds nations morally accountable even when he is sovereignly directing their actions. Both human responsibility and divine sovereignty are fully true at the same time.

sections.title: The Remnant Returns — Do Not Fear Assyria
sections.commentary:
In that day, the remnant of Israel will lean no longer on the one who struck them but on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. This is the conversion Isaiah has been calling for throughout: not a military solution but a theological one. Stop leaning on human empires and lean on God.

v. 20 — “In that day the remnant of Israel… will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.” The phrase in truth (or in faithfulness) distinguishes genuine trust from the religious performance Isaiah has already condemned. The remnant's reliance on God will not be ceremonial. It will be real.

The chapter closes with Assyria's army described as a great forest being cut down. And from Israel's devastated stump, a shoot will grow (11:1). The cutting down that looks like the end is, for God's people, the preparation for new growth.

keyVerse.quote: “Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!”
keyVerse.note: God is not reacting to Assyria's power by co-opting it; he is directing it. The world's dominant military superpower is a tool in the hand of the LORD. This does not make Assyria innocent — verses 12–19 make clear they will be judged for their pride. But it does make God sovereign over the most frightening human powers of every age.

10.theology: Divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Isaiah 10 raises the hardest question in theology with complete directness: how can God sovereignly direct the actions of wicked human agents and still hold those agents morally responsible for what they do? Isaiah does not resolve the tension but asserts both sides of it. God planned it; Assyria chose it; God will judge Assyria for it. Paul addresses the same tension in Romans 9 and offers the same response: the clay does not question the potter. The mystery is real, but its resolution lies in the character of the God who is both sovereign and just.
10.reflection: The two temptations this chapter addresses are the same ones Israel faced: leaning on the overwhelming power that threatens you, and despairing when that power seems unstoppable. God's word to the remnant (v. 24) is simply “do not be afraid.” The basis for that courage is not a better military assessment but a theological one: the LORD of hosts has a purpose, and no human empire is the last word in any situation. What is the ‘Assyria’ in your own life — the overwhelming power you are tempted either to appease or to despair before?
