11.subtitle: The Root of Jesse and the Peaceable Kingdom
11.intro: Overview. Chapter 11 is the great Messianic vision that follows the cutting down of the forest in chapter 10. From the stump of Jesse — the royal house reduced to near-extinction — a shoot will grow. The chapter describes the character of the coming king (vv. 1–5), the transformed creation over which he will reign (vv. 6–9), and the worldwide gathering of his people (vv. 10–16). It is one of the most complete portraits of the Messiah in all of Isaiah, and the New Testament draws on it repeatedly.

sections.title: The Shoot from the Stump of Jesse
sections.commentary:
The image of a shoot from the stump of Jesse is a study in divine reversals. The forest of chapter 10 is being cut down — mighty Assyria, and with it every human power that has set itself up against God. But from the stump that most people would consider finished, a shoot emerges. Jesse was David's father; by naming Jesse rather than David, Isaiah is reaching back past the royal dynasty to its humble root. The Messiah does not arrive at the height of the monarchy's glory but from its most reduced state.

v. 2 — “And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.” The six-fold description of the Spirit's work — wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear of the LORD — is the basis for the traditional Christian doctrine of the seven gifts of the Spirit (the LXX adds “piety” to the six). This is the equipment the Branch needs for his reign. At Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descends on him — the fulfillment of this verse (Matt 3:16).

Verses 3–5 describe a king who does not judge by appearances or rumours but by righteousness and faithfulness — whose verdicts are accurate because they are based on God's reality rather than human perception. The poor and meek will be vindicated; the wicked will be struck down. This is the justice the unjust legislators of chapter 10 refused to exercise — and that the Branch will establish forever.

sections.title: The Peaceable Kingdom
sections.commentary:
The famous images of wolf and lamb, leopard and goat, lion and calf lying down together have been debated as literal or metaphorical for centuries. What is not debatable is their intent: they describe the comprehensive transformation of creation under the reign of the Messiah. The predator-prey relationship — one of the most basic features of fallen nature — will be reversed. The wolf will not merely tolerate the lamb; they will share the same space.

The key to understanding the vision is verse 9: “They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.” The peace of the kingdom flows from the knowledge of God flooding the earth. Creation is transformed from within by the spread of the knowledge of its Creator. This is why Paul's vision of the redeemed creation in Romans 8 — creation “groaning” as it waits for the revelation of the sons of God — draws on exactly this imagery.

v. 9 — “The earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.” Habakkuk 2:14 quotes this verse almost exactly. It is the ultimate missionary vision: not a few scattered souls who know God, but the whole earth saturated with his knowledge as completely and universally as the sea covers the ocean floor.

sections.title: The Worldwide Gathering
sections.commentary:
“In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples — of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious.” Paul quotes verse 10 in Romans 15:12 as the foundation for his Gentile mission: the root of Jesse standing as a banner for the nations is the gospel going to the ends of the earth. What Isaiah saw as a future hope, Paul is enacting as present mission.

The gathering of the dispersed of Israel from the four corners of the earth (vv. 11–12) is both a near promise of return from exile and an ultimate promise of eschatological gathering that the exile only partially fulfils. The new exodus described in verses 15–16 — a highway for the remnant, the sea dried up — deliberately echoes the original Exodus. God's great redemptive acts follow a pattern: the original establishes the template; the later ones fulfil and surpass it.

keyVerse.quote: “And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The Spirit's resting on the Messiah is not temporary or intermittent but permanent — he rests on him. At Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descends and remains (John 1:32–33). The full range of Spirit-gifts needed for the Messiah's work — wisdom to teach, counsel to govern, might to deliver, knowledge and fear of God to judge rightly — are all present in him simultaneously and without measure (John 3:34).

11.theology:
The Messiah and the Spirit. Isaiah 11 is one of the foundational texts for the New Testament's understanding of the relationship between the Spirit and the Son. The Spirit does not supplement the Son's deity; he equips the Son's humanity for his mission. This is why Luke's Gospel emphasises the Spirit's activity throughout Jesus' ministry — at his conception, baptism, temptation, and first sermon (Luke 4:18, quoting Isaiah 61). The Spirit-filled Messiah is the model for all Spirit-filled ministry.

New creation. The peaceable kingdom of verses 6–9 is the Old Testament's most vivid description of what Scripture elsewhere calls the new creation. It is not simply a return to Eden but a transformation of the created order under the reign of the righteous King. This is why Revelation 21–22 draws on imagery from both Genesis and Isaiah: the new creation is both recovery and transcendence.
11.reflection: The shoot from Jesse's stump grows from a situation that looks finished. The dynasty is reduced; the forest has been cut down; the stump is all that remains. If you are in a season that feels like a stump — where what you had hoped for seems to have been cut off — Isaiah 11 is written for you. God's most significant growth often comes from the most apparently finished starting points.
11.text: <sup>1</sup>There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit. <sup>2</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD. <sup>3</sup>And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, <sup>4</sup>but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked. <sup>5</sup>Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins. <sup>6</sup>The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them. <sup>7</sup>The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. <sup>8</sup>The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. <sup>9</sup>They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. <sup>10</sup>In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples— of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious. <sup>11</sup>In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea. <sup>12</sup>He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. <sup>13</sup>The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim. <sup>14</sup>But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines to the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them. <sup>15</sup>And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals. <sup>16</sup>And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.

12.subtitle: A Song of Salvation
12.intro: Overview. Chapter 12 is a short hymn of praise — only six verses — that brings the first major section of Isaiah (chapters 1–12) to a doxological close. After eleven chapters of judgment, warning, and Messianic promise, the redeemed community breaks into song. The language draws on the Exodus (v. 2 quotes from the Song of Moses in Exodus 15) and looks forward to the gathering described at the end of chapter 11. This is what the people of God sound like when they have arrived at where God was always taking them.

sections.title: I Will Trust and Not Be Afraid
sections.commentary:
“You will say in that day: I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me.” The opening verse acknowledges that God's anger was real and deserved, and that his turning of it away is an act of pure grace. The song does not begin with innocence but with the acknowledgment of guilt forgiven. This is authentic praise: it knows what it has been forgiven from.

v. 2 — “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.” This is almost a direct quotation from the Song of Moses (Exod 15:2). Isaiah's redeemed community sings the same song as those who crossed the Red Sea — because they have experienced the same salvation. The new exodus has the same Redeemer.

Verse 3 — “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” — is the verse Jesus quotes in John 7:37–38 at the Feast of Tabernacles: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” The wells of salvation are not a future reality to be waited for; in Christ, they are open now.

sections.title: Make Known His Deeds Among the Peoples
sections.commentary: The second half of the hymn turns outward. Salvation received becomes mission declared: “Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted.” The redeemed community does not keep its salvation private. The glad shouting of verse 6 — “for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel” — echoes back to the trisagion of chapter 6, but now from the lips of the forgiven rather than the seraphim. The same holiness that undid Isaiah now becomes the ground of the community's joy. This is the arc of the entire gospel: the holy God who should destroy the sinner instead saves him, and the sinner worships.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.”
keyVerse.note: The word translated salvation is Yeshua — the same name as Jesus. “God is my Yeshua” is, in retrospect, a name as much as a statement. The song that brings the first section of Isaiah to a close is a song about the one who will bring all of God's purposes to their close.

12.reflection: Chapter 12 ends the first major section of Isaiah at the highest point imaginable: the redeemed community singing with joy, drawing from wells of salvation, declaring God's name among the nations. This is the destination God has been aiming at through all eleven chapters of judgment and promise. Whatever stage of the journey you are on, this is where it ends.
12.text: <sup>1</sup>You will say in that day: "I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. <sup>2</sup>Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation." <sup>3</sup>With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. <sup>4</sup>And you will say in that day: "Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted. <sup>5</sup>Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth. <sup>6</sup>Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."

13.subtitle: The Oracle Against Babylon
13.intro: Overview. Chapters 13–23 contain a series of oracles against the nations, beginning with Babylon. This is significant: Isaiah is prophesying the fall of Babylon more than a century before Babylon became a dominant power, and roughly two centuries before Cyrus of Persia conquered it in 539 BC. The oracle against Babylon serves a dual purpose — it announces specific historical judgment on a specific empire, and it uses that judgment as a lens through which to see the ultimate Day of the LORD against all that opposes God.

sections.title: Muster the Troops — The Day of the LORD Against Babylon
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with a battle summons: a banner raised, troops mustered, the gates of the nobles thrown open. But this is no ordinary war council — these are “my consecrated ones” and “my mighty warriors” (v. 3). God is the one assembling the army; the coming destruction of Babylon is his project. The language quickly escalates beyond any single historical event into the cosmic register of the Day of the LORD.

vv. 9–10 — “Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.” The cosmic darkness language — stars dimmed, sun darkened — recurs in the New Testament as a description of the last day (Matt 24:29; Rev 6:12–13). Isaiah's oracle against Babylon becomes a template for every ultimate divine judgment.

The pride of verse 11 is the specific charge: “I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant.” Babylon's sin is not merely military aggression but the arrogance of a power that has forgotten it is answerable to anyone. This is the sin of every empire, including the last.

sections.title: Babylon Fallen — Like Sodom and Gomorrah
sections.commentary: God will stir up the Medes against Babylon (v. 17) — a specific prophecy of the Persian-Median coalition that overthrew Babylon in 539 BC, fulfilled precisely. The description of abandoned Babylon in verses 19–22 — never inhabited, never settled, no Arab pitching his tent there, owls nesting, jackals lying down, ostriches dancing — uses exactly the imagery that Revelation 18 employs for the fall of the final Babylon. The historical fall of Babylon in the 6th century BC is a down-payment on the ultimate fall of everything that Babylon represents.

keyVerse.quote: “I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless.”
keyVerse.note: The oracle against one specific historical empire has this universal horizon: “I will punish the world.” Babylon is the instance; the world's arrogance is the charge. Every empire that mistakes its power for permanence is, in Isaiah's vision, standing where Babylon stood — and heading where Babylon went.

13.reflection: The oracles against the nations in Isaiah 13–23 are not comfortable reading, but they answer an urgent question: does God see what the nations are doing? Is there accountability beyond the reach of any earthly court? The answer of this chapter is unambiguous. The pomp of the arrogant has an expiry date set by God himself.
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. <sup>2</sup>On a bare mountain raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. <sup>3</sup>I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones. <sup>4</sup>The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle. <sup>5</sup>They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land. <sup>6</sup>Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! <sup>7</sup>Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. <sup>8</sup>They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame. <sup>9</sup>Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. <sup>10</sup>For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light. <sup>11</sup>I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless. <sup>12</sup>I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir. <sup>13</sup>Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger. <sup>14</sup>And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. <sup>15</sup>Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword. <sup>16</sup>Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished. <sup>17</sup>Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold. <sup>18</sup>Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children. <sup>19</sup>And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. <sup>20</sup>It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there. <sup>21</sup>But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. <sup>22</sup>Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.

14.subtitle: The Taunt Against the King of Babylon
14.intro: Overview. Chapter 14 continues the Babylon oracle with a taunt song addressed to the king of Babylon — one of the most dramatically vivid passages in all of Isaiah. The king who exalted himself to the heavens is brought down to Sheol; those who once cowered before him now mock him in death. The famous passage in verses 12–15 has been interpreted from the earliest centuries as a description of the fall of Satan, behind the earthly king. The chapter also contains brief oracles against Assyria and Philistia.

sections.title: The LORD Restores Israel
sections.commentary: Before the taunt song begins, Isaiah establishes its context: it is sung by a people who have been restored. The LORD will have compassion on Jacob, will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land (v. 1). The taunt song is not triumphalism arising from bitterness; it is the song of those who have been through the furnace of exile and have come out the other side. God's judgment on Babylon is inseparable from his restoration of his people. The fall of the oppressor and the freedom of the captives are the same event viewed from two directions.

sections.title: The Taunt Song: How You Are Fallen
sections.commentary:
The taunt song is a masterpiece of irony. The king who “made the world like a desert” (v. 17) now lies without a grave, trodden underfoot, while even the rulers of the nations receive honourable burial. The contrast between his living power and his dead helplessness is the point: all the greatness that seemed permanent and invincible is revealed in death to have been temporary and fragile.

vv. 12–14 — “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn!… You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high.’” The imagery here — the shining one (Helel ben Shachar, “Day Star, son of Dawn”) attempting to ascend above God's throne — has been read since the early church as the background to the fall of Satan (Luke 10:18; Rev 12:9). The earthly king of Babylon becomes a type of the spiritual power of pride itself: the will to self-exaltation that is the essence of all rebellion against God.

The five “I will” statements of verses 13–14 are the grammar of pride: I will ascend, I will set my throne, I will sit, I will ascend above the clouds, I will make myself like the Most High. Each one is the assertion of the self against the sovereignty of God. The verdict is verse 15: “But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit.” The higher the ascent claimed, the deeper the fall.

sections.title: Assyria and Philistia
sections.commentary: The chapter closes with brief oracles confirming that Assyria will be broken in God's land, and that Philistia should not rejoice too quickly at Judah's troubles. The oracle against Philistia contains a striking promise: “and the afflicted of his people will find refuge” (v. 32). Amid the oracles of judgment on the nations, the promise that God's own afflicted people have a place of refuge is a recurring refrain — the theme of the whole book compressed into a phrase.

keyVerse.quote: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high… I will make myself like the Most High.’”
keyVerse.note: The five “I will” statements are the grammar of pride at its most naked. Behind every act of human arrogance lies this claim: I will be my own ultimate authority. The king of Babylon is the extreme form of what is present in every sinful heart. This is why pride is not just a character flaw but a theological rebellion — it is the assertion of the self in the place of God.

14.reflection: The taunt song of Isaiah 14 is a meditation on the vanity of earthly greatness. The king who made the world tremble lies without a burial, mocked by those he once terrified. The chapter asks a searching question: in what are you tempted to place your ultimate confidence and identity? Because whatever it is, it has the same trajectory as the king of Babylon unless it is anchored in something that cannot fall.
14.text: <sup>1</sup>For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land, and sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob. <sup>2</sup>And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will possess them in the LORD's land as male and female slaves. They will take captive those who were their captors, and rule over those who oppressed them. <sup>3</sup>When the LORD has given you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve, <sup>4</sup>you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: "How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased! <sup>5</sup>The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of rulers, <sup>6</sup>that struck the peoples in wrath with unceasing blows, that ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution. <sup>7</sup>The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing. <sup>8</sup>The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, 'Since you were laid low, no woodcutter comes up against us.' <sup>9</sup>Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations. <sup>10</sup>All of them will speak and say to you: 'You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!' <sup>11</sup>Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers. <sup>12</sup>How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low! <sup>13</sup>You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; <sup>14</sup>I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.' <sup>15</sup>But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit. <sup>16</sup>Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you: 'Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, <sup>17</sup>who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?' <sup>18</sup>All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb; <sup>19</sup>but you are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch, clothed with the slain, those pierced by the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit, like a trampled corpse. <sup>20</sup>You will not be joined with them in burial, because you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. May the offspring of evildoers nevermore be named! <sup>21</sup>Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers, lest they rise and possess the earth, and fill the face of the world with cities." <sup>22</sup>I will rise up against them, declares the LORD of hosts, and will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, descendants and posterity, declares the LORD. <sup>23</sup>And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water, and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction, declares the LORD of hosts. <sup>24</sup>The LORD of hosts has sworn: "As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand, <sup>25</sup>that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains trample him underfoot; and his yoke shall depart from them, and his burden from their shoulder." <sup>26</sup>This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations. <sup>27</sup>For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? <sup>28</sup>In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle: <sup>29</sup>Rejoice not, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken, for from the serpent's root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent. <sup>30</sup>The firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy lie down in safety; but I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant it will slay. <sup>31</sup>Wail, O gate; cry out, O city; melt in fear, O Philistia, all of you! For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks. <sup>32</sup>What will one answer the messengers of the nation? "The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge."

15.subtitle: The Oracle Against Moab
15.intro: Overview. Chapters 15–16 form a single oracle against Moab, the nation east of the Dead Sea descended from Lot. The oracle is unusual in its tone: there is genuine mourning over Moab's destruction (15:5 — “My heart cries out for Moab”), and a remarkable invitation in 16:3–5 for Moab's fugitives to find shelter under Judah's king. Even in the oracles against the nations, Isaiah's God is not without compassion for the perishing.

sections.title: Moab Laid Waste
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with sudden destruction: “In a night Ar of Moab is laid waste and destroyed.” Town after town is named as the destruction spreads — Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh — a litany of places that had been centres of Moabite life now reduced to weeping and ruin. The people cut off their beards and shave their heads (signs of mourning) as the disaster rolls through the land.

v. 5 — “My heart cries out for Moab.” The speaker here is most naturally God himself (or Isaiah speaking for God). The God who judges Moab also mourns over Moab. This is not inconsistent — the same God who must deal with sin in justice also grieves over those who perish under that judgment. This theme reaches its fullest expression in Lamentations and in Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

keyVerse.quote: “My heart cries out for Moab.”
keyVerse.note: The brevity of this verse is part of its power. In the middle of an oracle announcing destruction, God's own heart cries out. Judgment and compassion are not mutually exclusive in God's character — they are simultaneously present. This is why the cross is simultaneously the most severe expression of divine justice and the most profound expression of divine love.

15.reflection: The oracles against the nations are often read only for their political and historical content. But Isaiah 15:5 breaks through that register entirely: God's heart cries out for the people he is judging. This should shape how God's people relate to those under judgment — not with triumph or indifference, but with the same broken compassion their God displays.
15.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone. <sup>2</sup>He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn; <sup>3</sup>in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears. <sup>4</sup>Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. <sup>5</sup>My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction; <sup>6</sup>the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more. <sup>7</sup>Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows. <sup>8</sup>For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim. <sup>9</sup>For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land.

16.subtitle: Moab's Pride and the Promise of the Throne
16.intro: Overview. Chapter 16 concludes the Moab oracle, moving from a remarkable offer of shelter for Moab's fugitives (vv. 1–5) through the description of Moab's pride (vv. 6–12) to the announcement of Moab's judgment within three years (vv. 13–14). The passage in verses 4–5 — describing a king who will judge in faithfulness and seek justice — is another of Isaiah's quiet Messianic insertions, pointing beyond any immediate political solution to the one king who will fully embody these qualities.

sections.title: Shelter for the Fugitives — A Messianic Glimpse
sections.commentary:
The opening verses offer something remarkable: an invitation for Moab's refugees to find shelter in Judah, and a call to Judah to hide the outcasts and not betray the fugitives (v. 3). In the middle of a judgment oracle, there is an offer of refuge. The fugitives fleeing destruction can find a hiding place under the wing of the Davidic king.

vv. 4–5 — “Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.” This description — a throne of steadfast love, faithfulness, justice, righteousness — cannot be fully satisfied by any historical Davidic king. It points to the one whose throne will be established for ever (9:7). Even in an oracle about Moab, Isaiah cannot help gesturing toward the king who will make everything right.

sections.title: Moab's Pride and Its Consequence
sections.commentary:
The reason Moab does not accept the offer of shelter is named plainly: “We have heard of the pride of Moab — how proud he is! — of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right” (v. 6). The offer of grace is refused because pride will not stoop to accept it. The specific sin of Moab is the same sin that brought down Babylon in chapter 14 — the refusal to acknowledge dependence and the insistence on self-sufficiency.

The mourning of verses 9–11 returns to the note struck in 15:5: genuine grief over Moab's harvest destroyed and its people desolate. The three-year timeline of verses 13–14 gives the oracle a deliberate specificity — this is not vague prophecy but a dated announcement that would soon be verifiable.

keyVerse.quote: “Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.”
keyVerse.note: The four qualities named — steadfast love, faithfulness, justice, righteousness — are the covenant attributes of God himself applied to the coming king. Every good king in Israel's history embodied them partially; the Messiah will embody them fully. This is the throne that will have no end (9:7).

16.reflection: Moab's refusal of the shelter offered in verse 3 is a parable of the pride that refuses grace. The offer is genuine; the shelter is real; the king on the throne of steadfast love is ready to receive. What prevents the fugitive from entering is not the absence of welcome but the presence of pride. This is always the obstacle.
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion. <sup>2</sup>Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon. <sup>3</sup>"Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; <sup>4</sup>let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land, <sup>5</sup>then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness." <sup>6</sup>We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right. <sup>7</sup>Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth. <sup>8</sup>For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea. <sup>9</sup>Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased. <sup>10</sup>And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting. <sup>11</sup>Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth. <sup>12</sup>And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail. <sup>13</sup>This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. <sup>14</sup>But now the LORD says, "In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble."

17.subtitle: The Oracle Against Damascus — and a Remnant Who Returns
17.intro: Overview. Chapter 17 contains an oracle against Damascus (the capital of Syria) and its ally Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel), who together formed the anti-Assyrian coalition of chapter 7. Their destruction is announced with the stark brevity of verses 1 and 3. But within the oracle of judgment, Isaiah inserts one of his characteristic remnant promises: a few survivors will look to their Maker, and those survivors will be like gleaned olives, like the stalk left after a harvest. The judgment produces a purified people.

sections.title: Damascus and Ephraim Fall
sections.commentary:
“Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins.” The oracle against Damascus is fulfilled in 732 BC when Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria destroys the city. Ephraim's alliance with Syria brings it the same fate: the northern kingdom falls to Assyria in 722 BC. The two powers that had made Ahaz's heart shake like trees in the wind (ch. 7) are themselves shown to have no more permanence than cities built on sand.

vv. 5–6 — “And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten — two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree.” The remnant is not impressive in number. Two or three berries at the top of the highest bough. But they are there. The harvest of judgment does not leave the tree entirely bare.

sections.title: The Remnant Looks to Their Maker
sections.commentary:
“In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel. He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands.” This is precisely the conversion that judgment is meant to produce. The people who in prosperity turned to their own idols and gardens (v. 10) will, in the fire of affliction, turn back to the one they had abandoned. Judgment is not the end of the story; it is the means by which the remnant is purified and restored to its true object.

Verse 10 names the cause of the disaster plainly: “you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge.” Forgetting God is not an intellectual failure but a moral and relational one — the deliberate neglect of the one who was always present and always sufficient.

keyVerse.quote: “In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: This is the goal of all of Isaiah's prophecy compressed into one verse. The point of every judgment oracle is not destruction but redirection — turning eyes that have been fixed on everything else back to the only one worth looking at. The Holy One of Israel is the beginning and end of all genuine recovery.

17.reflection: Chapter 17 sets the pattern that runs through all of Isaiah's national oracles: judgment that aims at restoration. The stripping of idols from the remnant is not punishment for its own sake but the loving removal of everything that was substituting for God. Where in your own life have you experienced the stripping of something you relied on — and found, on the other side, that your eyes were clearer for it?
17.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. <sup>2</sup>The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid. <sup>3</sup>The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts. <sup>4</sup>And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean. <sup>5</sup>And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. <sup>6</sup>Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten— two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel. <sup>7</sup>In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel. <sup>8</sup>He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense. <sup>9</sup>In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. <sup>10</sup>For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger, <sup>11</sup>though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain. <sup>12</sup>Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! <sup>13</sup>The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. <sup>14</sup>At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us.

18.subtitle: The Oracle Against Cush
18.intro: Overview. Chapter 18 is a brief oracle addressed to the land of Cush (ancient Ethiopia/Sudan), the nation from which Judah might have been tempted to seek military help against Assyria. The oracle is unusual in that it contains no explicit condemnation — it is more of a description of events, addressed to the distant Cushites, announcing that God is watching events unfold from his heavenly throne and will act at the right moment. The chapter ends with the remarkable promise that Cush will one day bring gifts to the LORD on Mount Zion.

sections.title: The LORD Watches from His Dwelling
sections.commentary:
The envoys from Cush — who apparently came to seek an alliance with Judah against Assyria — are sent back home with a message: go and wait. The imagery of verse 4 is striking: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” God is not inactive; he is watching with the quiet intensity of a farmer watching the sky in harvest season. The decisive moment will come, but not yet.

v. 4 — “I will quietly look from my dwelling.” The word quietly is the key. God does not need to be agitated or reactive. He watches with sovereign calm from his throne, knowing precisely when and how he will act. This is the posture of the God who “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph 1:11) — not hurried, not uncertain, not surprised.

Verse 7 closes with an eschatological promise: a people tall and smooth, from a land divided by rivers, will bring gifts to the LORD of hosts on Mount Zion. The oracle that begins with Cush being sent home ends with Cush making a pilgrimage. The rejected envoys become, in the end, worshippers. This anticipates Psalm 68:31 (“Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God”) and the Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.”
keyVerse.note: The image of God watching quietly from his dwelling is one of the most calming pictures of divine sovereignty in Scripture. It is not passivity — the harvest is coming and the pruning shears are ready (v. 5). It is the quiet confidence of one who is never caught off guard, never reactive, always working toward his own purposes at exactly the right pace.

18.reflection: Chapter 18 is a reminder that God's apparent silence is not absence. He is watching — quietly, intently, from his dwelling — and he will act at exactly the right moment. The temptation in every crisis is to rush ahead of God, to seek the Cushite alliance when God has told us to wait. The chapter invites trust in the God who watches before he acts.
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, <sup>2</sup>which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. <sup>3</sup>All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear! <sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest." <sup>5</sup>For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. <sup>6</sup>They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. <sup>7</sup>At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.

19.subtitle: The Oracle Against Egypt — and Egypt's Redemption
19.intro: Overview. Chapter 19 is one of the most astonishing chapters in all of Isaiah. It opens with a severe oracle against Egypt — civil war, failed Nile, economic collapse, foolish counsellors — and then pivots, in its second half, to one of the most remarkable promises in the Old Testament: Egypt will know the LORD, worship him, and be called “my people.” The chapter that begins with God riding on a swift cloud against Egypt ends with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel forming a threefold blessing in the earth.

sections.title: Judgment on Egypt
sections.commentary:
“Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them.” The God who dried up the Red Sea for Israel now comes against Egypt in its own land. The judgment is comprehensive: civil strife (v. 2), failed Nile (v. 5), dried-up canals, economic devastation, and — most cutting of all — counsellors made foolish. Egypt prided itself on its ancient wisdom; the princes of Zoan, sons of ancient kings, are made “utterly foolish” (v. 13).

v. 3 — “And the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers.” When divine wisdom is rejected, the vacuum is filled with the counterfeits — idols, sorcerers, mediums. The pattern is the same as in chapter 8:19. A nation that turns from God's word ends up consulting the dead for guidance.

sections.title: Egypt Will Know the LORD
sections.commentary:
The second half of the chapter is a series of “in that day” oracles that move from judgment to transformation. Five cities in Egypt will speak the language of Canaan (Hebrew) and swear allegiance to the LORD. An altar to the LORD in the heart of Egypt and a pillar at its border will be signs and witnesses to the LORD of hosts. And when Egyptians cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, he will send them a saviour and defend them — exactly as he did for Israel in Egypt.

v. 25 — “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.” These three nations — Egypt, the ancient enslaver of Israel; Assyria, the current oppressor; Israel, the covenant people — are placed side by side in a single blessing. The terms used of Israel throughout Scripture (“my people,” “the work of my hands,” “my heritage”) are distributed equally among all three. This is the most explicit anticipation of Gentile inclusion in the covenant in all of the Old Testament. Paul's mission to the nations is the fulfilment of this verse.

keyVerse.quote: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.”
keyVerse.note: The terms “my people” and “my heritage” are covenant terms used exclusively of Israel throughout the Old Testament. Here they are extended to Egypt and Assyria. This is not the abolition of Israel's election but its expansion — the covenant blessings flowing outward to the nations, exactly as God promised Abraham: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen 12:3).

19.theology: The universal scope of salvation. Isaiah 19:18–25 is the Old Testament's most explicit preview of what the New Testament calls the inclusion of the Gentiles. The nations that were Israel's greatest enemies — Egypt, Assyria — are called by the same covenant names as Israel herself. This does not mean that national identity is erased but that the covenant community is expanded. Paul's entire theology of Jew and Gentile in Ephesians 2–3 is the New Testament commentary on Isaiah 19.
19.reflection: Chapter 19 moves from “the LORD is coming against Egypt” to “blessed be Egypt my people” — from judgment to adoption, from terror to worship. This is the arc of the gospel for every human soul. The God who rides on a swift cloud against his enemies is the same God who says to those same enemies, “You are mine.” The distance between those two verses is the cross.
19.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them. <sup>2</sup>And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; <sup>3</sup>and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers; <sup>4</sup>and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts. <sup>5</sup>And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched, <sup>6</sup>and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. <sup>7</sup>There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more. <sup>8</sup>The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. <sup>9</sup>The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. <sup>10</sup>Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved. <sup>11</sup>The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against them. <sup>18</sup>In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction. <sup>19</sup>In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. <sup>20</sup>It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them. <sup>21</sup>And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them. <sup>22</sup>And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them. <sup>23</sup>In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. <sup>24</sup>In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth, <sup>25</sup>whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."

20.subtitle: The Sign of Isaiah's Nakedness
20.intro: Overview. Chapter 20 is a brief but vivid narrative. For three years, at God's command, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot as a living sign — a prophecy enacted in the prophet's own body. The sign had a specific target: Judah's temptation to rely on an Egyptian-Cushite military coalition against Assyria. Isaiah's three-year acted parable announced that Egypt and Cush would be led away by Assyria as naked prisoners, and therefore they were no foundation to build on.

sections.title: Three Years Naked and Barefoot
sections.commentary:
The chapter is anchored by the historical detail of Sargon II of Assyria's campaign against Ashdod (711 BC), confirming the oracle's specific context. Isaiah's three-year walking sign was a sustained, public, costly demonstration — not a brief prophetic gesture but a years-long embodiment of the message. The prophet's body became the sermon.

v. 3 — “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush.” The word servant here connects Isaiah to the Servant figure of chapters 40–55. Isaiah's willingness to suffer public shame to deliver God's message is itself a foreshadowing of the greater Servant who would bear far greater shame for a far greater purpose.

The practical point of the sign is verse 6: those who were looking to Egypt and Cush for help will be horrified when those powers are themselves led away as prisoners. “And we, how shall we escape?” The question is the point. If your source of security has been captured, what are you left with? Isaiah's answer, consistent throughout the book, is that the only reliable refuge has always been the LORD himself.

keyVerse.quote: “And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?’”
keyVerse.note: The question “how shall we escape?” is the exact question every misplaced confidence eventually produces. When the thing we trusted — whether Egypt, an alliance, a financial plan, a relationship — fails, we are left with the question Isaiah has been asking from chapter 1: to whom are you actually looking? The answer the book provides is always the same: “Look to the rock from which you were hewn” (51:1).

20.reflection: Isaiah's three-year acted sign is a reminder that God sometimes calls his servants to costly, public, apparently undignified forms of witness. The prophet did not get to choose a more respectable way to deliver this message. The question the chapter poses is both historical and personal: what is the Egypt or Cush in your own life — the security that looks impressive but will one day be led away in chains?
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it— <sup>2</sup>at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. <sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, <sup>4</sup>so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt. <sup>5</sup>Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. <sup>6</sup>And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"

21.subtitle: Oracles Against Babylon, Edom, and Arabia
21.intro: Overview. Chapter 21 contains three short oracles, each addressed to a different nation. The first and longest (vv. 1–10) is a vision of Babylon’s fall, delivered with such physical intensity that the prophet reels under it. The second (vv. 11–12) is a night-watchman exchange with Edom — poetic, cryptic, unresolved. The third (vv. 13–17) turns to the desert caravans of Arabia, where the commerce of the ancient world will be silenced within a year. Together they form a triptych: the great empire, its anxious neighbor, and the ordinary trader — all subject to the same sovereign word.

sections.title: The Fall of Babylon
sections.commentary:
The oracle opens with a locust-like storm sweeping in from the wilderness — the image of an invading army in Isaiah’s symbolic vocabulary. God commands the Medes and Elamites to besiege, and Isaiah, caught up in the vision, reacts with physical anguish: his body shakes, his mind is dismayed, the twilight he longed for has become terror. The prophet is not a detached analyst but a participant in what he sees. He watches a banqueting table become a battlefield.

v. 3 — “My loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor.” The image of labor pains for divine judgment runs throughout Isaiah (13:8; 26:17; 66:7) and into the New Testament (Matt. 24:8). It conveys both inevitability and agony: what is coming cannot be stopped, and it will not be painless.

The watchman’s announcement — “Fallen, fallen is Babylon” — is laconic and precise. Revelation 18:2 quotes it exactly, applying it to the final fall of the city that represents human empire in all ages. Isaiah sees it as already done; the prophetic perfect collapses the distance between announcement and event. The chapter closes with a word of suffering comfort to “my threshed one, son of my threshing floor” — Israel, ground down but not destroyed, told that this vision is for them.

sections.title: The Watchman of Edom
sections.commentary: Someone calls from Seir (Edom): “Watchman, what time of the night?” The question has an anxious edge — is the darkness nearly over? The watchman’s reply is the most enigmatic in Isaiah: “Morning comes, and also the night. If you would inquire, inquire; come back again.” There is light coming, but darkness too. Not a promise of dawn without night, but a summons to keep inquiring. Edom is told it may return with its question — which is itself a mercy: the door is not closed.

sections.title: Arabia
sections.commentary: The final oracle addresses the caravans of Dedan and the people of Tema, who are called to bring water and bread to the fleeing refugees of Kedar. The judgment on Kedar — the Arabian tribes whose archers and warriors were renowned — is precise: within one year, “all the glory of Kedar will come to an end.” The timeframe is specific, and God underwrites it with his own name. Even the edges of the ancient world are within the scope of his word.

keyVerse.quote: “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night? The watchman says: ‘Morning comes, and also the night.’”
keyVerse.note: The exchange is one of the strangest moments in prophetic literature. But its strangeness is the point: history does not move in simple arcs from darkness to light. Morning and night come together. The right response is not resignation but inquiry — keep asking, keep returning.

21.reflection: Isaiah reeled physically under the vision of Babylon’s fall. The prophets were not spectators of history but participants in God’s grief over it. Is there a situation in the world right now that you have allowed yourself to feel — not just analyze? And what does it mean to keep “inquiring” in the darkness when the watchman can only say that morning and night will both come?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land. <sup>2</sup>A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end. <sup>3</sup>Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see. <sup>4</sup>My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling. <sup>5</sup>They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield! <sup>6</sup>For thus the Lord said to me: "Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees. <sup>7</sup>When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently." <sup>8</sup>Then he who saw cried out: "Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights. <sup>9</sup>And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground." <sup>10</sup>O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you. <sup>11</sup>The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, "Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?" <sup>12</sup>The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again." <sup>13</sup>The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. <sup>14</sup>To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema. <sup>15</sup>For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle. <sup>16</sup>For thus the Lord said to me, "Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end. <sup>17</sup>And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken."

22.subtitle: The Valley of Vision
22.intro: Overview. Chapter 22 is unique in the oracles-against-the-nations sequence: it is addressed not to a foreign power but to Jerusalem itself, here called “the valley of vision.” The city that has received more revelation than any other is judged precisely for what it did with it. The occasion appears to be a near-miss — perhaps Sennacherib’s siege in 701 BC, when the city was threatened and then inexplicably spared. But instead of weeping and repentance, Jerusalem breaks out in celebration. The chapter also contains a striking personal oracle against the arrogant royal steward Shebna, and a promise about a better servant, Eliakim.

sections.title: The Unrepentant City
sections.commentary:
The rooftops of Jerusalem are full of noise and celebration. The prophet asks: what has happened that everyone has gone up to the housetops? The answer comes with heavy irony: your slain were not killed by the sword or in battle — they fled and were taken. The city’s leaders ran, its defenders scattered. Yet now they celebrate as if they had won.

Isaiah weeps, and asks to be left alone in his grief. He refuses to be comforted. This is not performance but prophetic solidarity with what God sees: a day of tumult, of trampling, of confusion. The Assyrian (or Babylonian) army has assembled; the siege equipment is in place; the city’s own water system has been inspected and prepared. Everything is ready for judgment — and Jerusalem parties.

v. 13 — “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Paul quotes this exact phrase in 1 Cor. 15:32 as the logical conclusion of a life with no resurrection. Isaiah identifies it not as honest hedonism but as hardened unresponsiveness — the refusal to hear what God is saying in the events of the day.

The verdict in verse 14 is solemn: “This iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die.” Some sins have a point of no return — not because forgiveness is impossible in principle, but because the heart has crossed a threshold of deliberate, celebratory rejection of what is plainly true.

sections.title: Shebna and Eliakim
sections.commentary:
The oracle pivots from the city to one man: Shebna, the steward (literally “the one over the house”), who has been cutting himself a grand tomb on the heights. He is building his memorial while the city burns. God will take him up like a ball and hurl him into a wide land, and he will die there far from home. His grand tomb will be empty.

In his place God will call Eliakim, on whom he will hang “the key of the house of David” — authority to open and shut, to admit and exclude. Revelation 3:7 applies this language directly to Christ: “the words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens.” Eliakim is a type whose antitype fills the office perfectly.

v. 22 — “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David.” A key on the shoulder was a mark of stewardship over the royal household — physical, weighty, impossible to overlook. The image passes through Isaiah into Revelation as the defining picture of Christ’s absolute authority over access to God.

keyVerse.quote: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.”
keyVerse.note: What begins as a personnel change in Hezekiah’s court becomes one of the richest Christological images in the Old Testament. Rev. 3:7 places this language on the lips of the risen Christ. No one approaches the Father except through him; no one is excluded who comes through him.

22.reflection: Jerusalem celebrated survival without repentance. The near-miss became a party rather than a turning point. Is there a situation in your life where God has been merciful and you have responded with relief rather than return? What would true repentance look like in that situation now?
22.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning the valley of vision. What do you mean that you have gone up, all of you, to the housetops, <sup>2</sup>you who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town? Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle. <sup>3</sup>All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured. All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away. <sup>4</sup>Therefore I said: "Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people." <sup>5</sup>For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains. <sup>6</sup>And Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. <sup>7</sup>Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates. <sup>8</sup>He has taken away the covering of Judah. In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest, <sup>9</sup>and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many. You collected the waters of the lower pool, <sup>10</sup>and you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. <sup>11</sup>You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago. <sup>12</sup>In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth; <sup>13</sup>and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine. "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." <sup>14</sup>The LORD of hosts has revealed himself in my ears: "Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die," says the Lord GOD of hosts. <sup>15</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD of hosts, "Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household, and say to him: <sup>16</sup>What have you to do here, and whom have you here, that you have cut out here a tomb for yourself, you who cut out a tomb on the height and carve a dwelling for yourself in the rock? <sup>17</sup>Behold, the LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man. He will seize firm hold on you <sup>18</sup>and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land. There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house. <sup>19</sup>I will thrust you from your office, and you will be pulled down from your station. <sup>20</sup>In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, <sup>21</sup>and I will clothe him with your robe, and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand. And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. <sup>22</sup>And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. <sup>23</sup>And I will fasten him like a peg in a secure place, and he will become a throne of honor to his father's house. <sup>24</sup>And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons. <sup>25</sup>In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off, for the LORD has spoken."

23.subtitle: The Oracle Against Tyre
23.intro: Overview. Tyre was the commercial capital of the ancient world — the great Phoenician port whose ships connected Egypt, Canaan, Spain, and the Greek islands. Its fall would be like the collapse of a global financial center. Isaiah’s oracle against it (the last of the series begun in chapter 13) is not merely a military prediction but a theological meditation: what happens when the city that made itself indispensable is removed? The chapter ends with a surprising note: after seventy years, Tyre’s commerce will resume — and its profits will be consecrated to the LORD.

sections.title: The Fall of the Merchant City
sections.commentary:
Ships returning to Tyre from Tarshish (likely Spain, the far western edge of the known world) will find no harbor, no house, no city. The news reaches Cyprus; it reaches Egypt; the sea itself mourns. Tyre is called “the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes” — a city so wealthy it made kings. Now its makers of purple cloth are silent.

The agent of judgment is Babylon (v. 13), whose armies will lay siege and bring it down. The theological point is pressed in verse 9: the LORD of hosts has planned it, “to defile the pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth.” Tyre is not judged for being a trading city but for the pride that made commerce an end in itself — the assumption that prosperity is self-generated and self-sustaining.

v. 9 — “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pride of all glory.” This phrase gathers the entire oracles-against-the-nations sequence into one sentence. The common thread in Babylon, Assyria, Moab, and Tyre is pride — the assumption that human achievement is the ultimate story. God’s purpose, running through all these judgments, is to defile that assumption.

sections.title: Seventy Years and Restoration
sections.commentary:
After seventy years — an echo of Jeremiah’s number for Babylon’s dominion — Tyre will be forgotten and then restored. Isaiah uses a striking metaphor: Tyre will be like a forgotten prostitute, taking up her harp and singing to attract customers again, going back to her trade. The image is deliberately undignified: commerce for its own sake is not ennobled by its resumption.

But the oracle ends with an unexpected consecration: Tyre’s profits will not be stored for itself but will be “holy to the LORD” and used to feed those who dwell before him. Commerce redeemed becomes service. The wealth of the nations, purged of its pride, flows at last toward God. It is a small seed of the larger vision in Isaiah 60–62.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth.”
keyVerse.note: The oracles against the nations are not vindictive but clarifying. God is not against cities or commerce; he is against the pride that refuses to acknowledge him as the source of all prosperity. Every judgment in chapters 13–23 is a reorientation of glory toward its proper object.

23.reflection: Tyre’s commerce was eventually consecrated rather than abolished. God’s goal is not the destruction of human achievement but its reorientation. What gifts, skills, or resources in your life are currently operating for self-glorification — and what would it look like to consecrate them?
23.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor! From the land of Cyprus it is revealed to them. <sup>2</sup>Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you. <sup>3</sup>And on many waters your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile; you were the merchant of the nations. <sup>4</sup>Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea, saying: "I have neither labored nor given birth, I have neither reared young men nor brought up young women." <sup>5</sup>When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre. <sup>6</sup>Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coast! <sup>7</sup>Is this your exultant city whose origin is from days of old, whose feet carried her to settle far away? <sup>8</sup>Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth? <sup>9</sup>The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth. <sup>10</sup>Cross over your land like the Nile, O daughter of Tarshish; there is no restraint anymore. <sup>11</sup>He has stretched out his hand over the sea; he has shaken the kingdoms; the LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds. <sup>12</sup>And he said: "You will no more exult, O oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon; arise, cross over to Cyprus, even there you will have no rest." <sup>13</sup>Behold the land of the Chaldeans! This is the people that was not; Assyria destined it for wild beasts. They erected their siege towers, they stripped her palaces bare, they made her a ruin. <sup>14</sup>Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste. <sup>15</sup>In that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king. At the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute: <sup>16</sup>"Take a harp; go about the city, O forgotten prostitute! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered." <sup>17</sup>At the end of seventy years, the LORD will visit Tyre, and she will return to her wages and will prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth. <sup>18</sup>Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD. It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD.

24.subtitle: The LORD’s Devastation of the Earth
24.intro: Overview. With chapter 24 the focus widens dramatically from individual nations to the whole earth. Sometimes called the “Isaiah Apocalypse,” chapters 24–27 form a distinct unit dealing with universal judgment and ultimate renewal. Chapter 24 describes the desolation of the earth in terms that deliberately echo the flood narrative — a covenant broken, creation undone — before closing with a vision of the LORD reigning on Mount Zion. It is not primarily about a specific historical event but about the logic of history itself: what happens when human civilization persistently violates the terms of its existence.

sections.title: The Earth Laid Waste
sections.commentary:
The opening is sweeping and egalitarian in the worst possible way: God will empty the earth and twist its surface, and it will be the same for everyone — priest and people, master and servant, buyer and seller, lender and borrower. All social distinctions collapse under universal judgment. The reason is given in verse 5: the earth is defiled under its inhabitants “because they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant.” The language draws on Noahic covenant categories: the earth’s desolation is the consequence of civilization’s persistent rejection of its creaturely status.

v. 5 — “The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant.” The “everlasting covenant” here is almost certainly the Noahic covenant (Gen. 9:1–17), which bound all humanity, not just Israel. The judgment is universal because the violation is universal — not ethnic but human.

The joy of the city has ceased, the wine dries up, the music stops. In the middle of chapter 24 there is a haunting image: in the city of chaos, the gates are battered into desolation. “For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done” — the remnant image again. Something is left, but barely.

sections.title: Songs in the Midst of Judgment
sections.commentary:
