From the west, voices lift up. From the east, they glorify the LORD. From the coastlands: “Glory to the Righteous One.” Isaiah hears these and collapses: “But I say, I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me!” The contrast is jarring — songs of praise interrupted by the prophet’s grief at the ongoing treachery of those still on the earth. The praises are real and deserved; the grief is also real and warranted. The two exist together until the judgment is complete.

The chapter ends with cosmic upheaval — the host of heaven and the kings of the earth gathered, imprisoned, punished. Then: “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.” The chapter that began with universal desolation ends with God on his throne. The devastation is not the last word; the reign is.

v. 23 — “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem.” This anticipates the great vision of chapters 65–66 and the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21–22. All the oracles against the nations — all the demolition of human pride — have been in service of this: the earth cleared for God’s unchallenged reign.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders, for the LORD of hosts will reign.”
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of comprehensive devastation, this sentence arrives like a foundation stone. The point of all the undoing is not nihilism but preparation — the clearing of the earth for the reign that cannot be shaken. It is the same movement John sees in Revelation: the bowls of wrath followed by the marriage supper of the Lamb.

24.theology: Creation, Covenant, and Judgment. Chapter 24 ties judgment to covenant violation in creation terms, not merely national terms. The “everlasting covenant” of verse 5 reaches back to Noah and forward to all humanity. This is not Israel’s judgment but the world’s judgment — grounded in the creational order that God established and humanity persistently subverts. Reformed theology has always insisted that general revelation leaves all people without excuse (Rom. 1:20), and Isaiah 24 shows what that accountability looks like at scale.
24.reflection: Isaiah hears songs of praise and immediately collapses in grief — both responses are appropriate to the same reality. How do you hold together genuine worship with honest lament over the state of the world? Which comes more naturally to you, and which do you need to cultivate?
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants. <sup>2</sup>And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor. <sup>3</sup>The earth shall be utterly empty and utterly plundered; for the LORD has spoken this word. <sup>4</sup>The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and withers; the highest people of the earth languish. <sup>5</sup>The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant. <sup>6</sup>Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt; therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched, and few men are left. <sup>7</sup>The wine mourns, the vine languishes, all the merry-hearted sigh. <sup>8</sup>The mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled. <sup>9</sup>No more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it. <sup>10</sup>The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter. <sup>11</sup>There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished. <sup>12</sup>Desolation is left in the city; the gates are battered into ruins. <sup>13</sup>For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done. <sup>14</sup>They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west. <sup>15</sup>Therefore in the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. <sup>16</sup>From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One. But I say, "I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed." <sup>17</sup>Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth! <sup>18</sup>He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble. <sup>19</sup>The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken. <sup>20</sup>The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again. <sup>21</sup>On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth. <sup>22</sup>They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished. <sup>23</sup>Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.

25.subtitle: A Feast on the Mountain
25.intro: Overview. Chapter 25 is one of the high points of Isaiah — a psalm of praise for what God has done and will do, including two of the most stunning promises in the Old Testament: the abolition of death and the wiping away of every tear. After the cosmic devastation of chapter 24, God throws a banquet. The chapter also contains a compact oracle against Moab (vv. 10–12), which serves as a foil to highlight the contrast between those who trust in the LORD and those who trust in their own strength.

sections.title: Praise for the Faithful God
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with first-person praise: “O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you.” It is notable that individual praise comes here, after the widest-angle vision of chapters 13–24. The movement is not from personal piety to cosmic concern but the reverse: having seen what God will do to the whole earth, the prophet responds personally. The grounds for praise are specific: God has done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. The destroyed city (the fortified city of the nations, v. 2) becomes a heap; the strong peoples glorify him; the ruthless nations fear him.

Verses 4–5 describe what God has been to the poor and needy: a stronghold, a shelter from the storm, shade from the heat. When the ruthless come like a winter rainstorm, God is the wall that deflects them. The theology of divine protection is always concrete in Isaiah: not abstract comfort but a specific interposition between the vulnerable and the force bearing down on them.

sections.title: The Feast, the Veil, and the Death of Death
sections.commentary:
On this mountain — Zion, the place of God’s reign — God will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine. The universality is emphatic: for all peoples, for all nations. The banquet that was only available to Israel in its fullest form is opened to everyone. John’s vision of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9) is the New Testament realization of this promise.

v. 7 — “He will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations.” The veil is interpretive: it is the darkness of ignorance and spiritual blindness that prevents people from seeing reality as it is. Paul picks up this language in 2 Cor. 3:14–16, speaking of the veil over the heart that is removed in Christ. The feast and the lifting of the veil belong together: to eat at God’s table is to see clearly.

Verse 8 stands among the most important sentences in the Old Testament: “He will swallow up death forever.” Paul quotes it directly in 1 Corinthians 15:54 as the word that is fulfilled in the resurrection of Christ. And then: “The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces.” John echoes it in Revelation 21:4. These are not figures of speech; they are the literal program of what God intends to do. Death will not be managed or mitigated but swallowed — consumed by something greater than itself.

sections.title: Moab as Foil
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with a brief, harsh oracle against Moab, who is described as a swimmer flailing in a dunghill. The contrast with the feast is deliberate: those who feast on the mountain are those who trusted the LORD; Moab, representing self-sufficient pride, finds its fortifications brought low and trampled. The joy of verses 6–9 and the judgment of verses 10–12 are two sides of the same reality: the same God who prepares the feast also brings down the proud.

keyVerse.quote: “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth.”
keyVerse.note: This is one of the clearest resurrection promises in the entire Old Testament. “Swallow up death forever” is the language of total, permanent defeat — not death postponed but death ended. Paul places it at the climax of his resurrection argument (1 Cor. 15:54), and John plants it at the center of the new creation (Rev. 21:4). The whole trajectory of redemptive history bends toward this sentence.

25.theology: The Death of Death. Isaiah 25:8 stands at the foundation of the biblical doctrine of resurrection and new creation. It is not a metaphor for spiritual renewal but a literal promise about the fate of death itself. Reformed theology has always held that bodily resurrection is not an add-on to salvation but its culmination — the restoration of the whole person in a redeemed creation. The feast of verse 6 is the eschatological Eucharist, the wedding supper of the Lamb, the culmination of all that the covenant has been building toward. Timothy Keller often noted that Christianity is unique in offering not escape from the material world but its transformation — Isaiah 25 is one of the oldest and clearest biblical grounds for that claim.
25.reflection: God’s response to the devastation of chapter 24 is a banquet. Not a repair program or a recovery plan — a feast. What does it tell you about God that his ultimate answer to the brokenness of the world is abundance and celebration? And which promise from this chapter do you most need to hold onto right now: the feast, the lifted veil, or the end of death and tears?
25.text: <sup>1</sup>O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. <sup>2</sup>For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin; the foreigners' palace is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. <sup>3</sup>Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you. <sup>4</sup>For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat; for the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall, <sup>5</sup>like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down. <sup>6</sup>On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined. <sup>7</sup>And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations. <sup>8</sup>He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken. <sup>9</sup>It will be said on that day, "Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation." <sup>10</sup>For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill. <sup>11</sup>And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands. <sup>12</sup>And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust.

26.subtitle: The Song of the Strong City
26.intro: Overview. Chapter 26 is a sustained song — partly communal, partly prophetic — celebrating the security of those who trust in the LORD while the lofty city of the nations lies in the dust. It includes one of the clearest Old Testament anticipations of bodily resurrection (v. 19), framed within a meditation on the contrast between God’s reliable character and human weakness. The chapter invites Israel to enter her chambers and wait while God’s judgment passes — an echo of Passover, a foretaste of the final hiding.

sections.title: The City That Trusts
sections.commentary:
The strong city of Israel is contrasted with the lofty city of the nations brought down in chapter 25. What makes the strong city strong is not its walls but its trust: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.” The Hebrew is shalom shalom — doubled peace, complete peace — for the mind (yetser, inclination or imagination) that is stayed on God.

v. 3 — “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.” John MacArthur noted that the word stayed implies something leaning on God for support — not passive acceptance but active, sustained reliance. The peace is not the absence of trouble but a stability that the trouble cannot reach.

Verses 7–9 are among the most honest statements of desire in the entire Bible: “My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you.” The desire for God is itself the fruit of God’s character becoming visible through judgment — when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.

sections.title: Human Weakness and God’s Power
sections.commentary:
The middle section is brutally honest about Israel’s limitations. The wicked do not learn righteousness even when shown grace; they do not see God’s majesty. And Israel itself has accomplished nothing: “We have not achieved any deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen.” The labor-pain image returns: like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out but bears only wind. All of Israel’s effort at self-salvation has produced nothing.

This is not despair but preparation — the emptying that precedes the divine act. God does not share the rescue with a secondary agent; the deliverance must come entirely from him, precisely because human strength has exhausted itself trying.

sections.title: Your Dead Shall Live
sections.commentary:
Into the confession of human futility God speaks: “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!” The resurrection here is explicitly bodily — bodies, dust, awakening. It is addressed to those who have died in covenant with the LORD. The dew of God will fall on the land of the dead and give life. This is not mere national restoration but the earliest clear promise of individual bodily resurrection in Isaiah.

v. 19 — “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise.” The passage is directly in line with Daniel 12:2 (“many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake”) and forms the Old Testament ground for what Paul will develop fully in 1 Corinthians 15. Those who died having produced only wind (v. 18) will be raised by God’s dew (v. 19) — the reversal is total.

The chapter closes with a call to hide: “Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by.” The Passover echo is unmistakable — blood on the doorpost, God passing through to judge, the hidden people emerging into the morning of salvation.

keyVerse.quote: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.”
keyVerse.note: The doubled shalom — peace-peace — is not accidental. It indicates completeness: there is no dimension of a person’s life that this peace does not reach. And it is entirely relational — it belongs to the one whose imagination is anchored in God, not in circumstances. Philippians 4:7 is the New Testament cognate: the peace of God that guards heart and mind in Christ Jesus.

26.reflection: The people in this chapter are told to enter their chambers and hide “for a little while.” There is a season of patient waiting in the darkness that belongs to the life of faith. Where are you right now — in a waiting season, a labor season, or a morning-after season? And what does “staying your mind on God” actually look like in the middle of it?
26.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: "We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. <sup>2</sup>Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in. <sup>3</sup>You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. <sup>4</sup>Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock. <sup>5</sup>For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust. <sup>6</sup>The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy." <sup>7</sup>The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous. <sup>8</sup>In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul. <sup>9</sup>My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness. <sup>10</sup>If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD. <sup>11</sup>O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them. <sup>12</sup>O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works. <sup>13</sup>O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance. <sup>14</sup>They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them. <sup>15</sup>But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land. <sup>16</sup>O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them. <sup>17</sup>Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD; <sup>18</sup>we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen. <sup>19</sup>Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead. <sup>20</sup>Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by. <sup>21</sup>For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain.

27.subtitle: The Great Harvest
27.intro: Overview. Chapter 27 concludes the Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24–27) with three movements: the defeat of the serpentine powers (v. 1), the song of the vineyard revisited (vv. 2–6), and the ingathering of scattered Israel (vv. 12–13). It stands in deliberate contrast with chapter 5’s vineyard song — the same vineyard, but now God tends it with care and there is fruit. The chapter is eschatological: it looks to the final outcome of history.

sections.title: Leviathan Defeated
sections.commentary: A single verse, but a thunderclap: on that day, the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and will slay the dragon that is in the sea. Three designations for the same chaos-monster — the ancient Near Eastern symbol of cosmic disorder, rebellion against creation, the power behind human empires. In Revelation 12–13, John identifies this figure as the dragon who is the Devil and Satan. The sword of the LORD ends what began in the garden.

sections.title: The Vineyard Song Reversed
sections.commentary:
Chapter 5 opened with a vineyard song that ended in destruction: the wall torn down, the vineyard given to thorns. Here the song begins again, but God’s posture has changed: “I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day.” God is now the attentive gardener, not the disappointed owner. His anger has gone; he longs to make peace.

v. 4 — “I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me.” The urgency of the repeated “make peace with me” is striking. God is not waiting to be asked; he is pressing the offer. The thorn-and-brier threat has no target if the people will only turn and accept the peace.

Israel, by contrast, will send out its roots and fill the whole world with fruit (v. 6) — the vine that was to fill the land now fills the earth. This is the mission vision of Isaiah 19 and 60 in compressed form.

sections.title: The Ingathering
sections.commentary: The section closes with an image of harvest and return. God will thresh from the River to the Brook of Egypt, and the scattered ones will be gathered “one by one” — not in masses but individually, personally known and retrieved. A great trumpet will sound, and those lost in Assyria and Egypt will come and worship on the holy mountain. The apocalypse ends not in cosmic wreckage but in pilgrimage and praise.

keyVerse.quote: “In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.”
keyVerse.note: The vine that was stripped in chapter 5 becomes the vine that fills the earth. This is the covenantal logic of Isaiah in miniature: judgment clears the way for new growth, and the new growth exceeds the old. It is also a Christological verse: Jesus declares himself the true vine (John 15:1), and his fruitfulness fills the world through those who abide in him.

27.reflection: God says “I have no wrath” and doubles the invitation: “let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me.” There is urgency in the repetition — not threat, but longing. In what area of your life have you been treating God’s patience as distance rather than invitation?
27.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea. <sup>2</sup>In that day, "A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! <sup>3</sup>I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day; <sup>4</sup>I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. <sup>5</sup>Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me." <sup>6</sup>In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit. <sup>7</sup>Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain? <sup>8</sup>Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind. <sup>9</sup>Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing. <sup>10</sup>For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches. <sup>11</sup>When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor. <sup>12</sup>In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel. <sup>13</sup>And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

28.subtitle: Woe to the Drunkards of Ephraim
28.intro: Overview. With chapter 28, Isaiah moves from the oracles-against-the-nations and the apocalypse into a new section of woes (chs. 28–33), directed primarily against Judah’s leaders for their catastrophic political strategy: seeking alliance with Egypt against Assyria rather than trusting in the LORD. Chapter 28 opens with a woe against the northern kingdom (Ephraim/Samaria), already fallen or falling, then turns to Jerusalem’s leaders — drunk priests and prophets who have made a “covenant with death.” It contains the foundational cornerstone promise (vv. 16–17) and the unforgettable image of a bed too short to stretch out on.

sections.title: The Fading Flower of Ephraim
sections.commentary:
The woe against Ephraim opens with a vivid image: the drunkard’s crown, glorious in its beauty, is like the first ripe fig of summer — whoever sees it swallows it immediately. The northern kingdom is beautiful, conspicuous, and already doomed. Assyria will come and trample it. But through the wreckage God himself will be a crown of glory and a diadem of beauty to the remnant — the contrast between the fading wreath of human pride and the unfading crown of divine presence.

The Judean priests and prophets are then addressed — and they too are drunk: reeling in their visions, stumbling in their judgments, vomiting over their tables. Their response to Isaiah’s preaching is sarcastic mockery: who is he to teach us? Are we children? Line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little, there a little — the kind of rote instruction given to infants. God accepts the characterization: fine, since you won’t listen to clear Hebrew, you will learn through the incomprehensible language of foreign conquerors. The very thing they mocked as elementary becomes the instrument of their undoing.

vv. 9–10 — The priests’ mockery is one of the most poignant moments in Isaiah. They had received more revelation than any generation — and dismissed it as baby talk. Paul reflects on this dynamic in 1 Cor. 14:21, quoting Isaiah 28:11: foreign tongues become a sign, not to believers, but to unbelievers.

sections.title: The Covenant with Death and the Cornerstone
sections.commentary:
Jerusalem’s rulers have made “a covenant with death” and “an agreement with Sheol.” The language is startling — Isaiah is naming their political strategy (the Egyptian alliance) for what it actually is: a bargain with the powers that kill. They believe the overwhelming scourge will pass them by because of this deal. God pronounces their lie exposed.

Against it he sets the cornerstone: “Behold, I am the one who has laid in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: ‘Whoever believes will not be in haste.’” Peter (1 Pet. 2:6) and Paul (Rom. 9:33; 10:11) both quote this verse as fulfilled in Christ — the cornerstone against whom others stumble but in whom believers find the only sure foundation. Justice will be the measuring line; righteousness the plumb line. Everything built on other foundations will be swept away.

v. 20 — “For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in.” A memorable image of Egypt as a security blanket: it cannot actually cover you. Every alliance that substitutes for trust in God will prove too small for the crisis it was supposed to manage.

sections.title: The Parable of the Farmer
sections.commentary: The chapter ends with an unexpected parable from agriculture: the farmer does not plow endlessly, does not thresh every grain the same way, does not run the cartwheel over every crop. He knows that different plants require different tools, and he knows when to stop. This wisdom, Isaiah says, comes from God: “His God instructs him and teaches him the right way.” The point is subversive: if God has the wisdom to vary his means in farming, does he not also vary his means in judgment? The Assyrian invasion is not the end of the story; the threshing is proportioned to the grain, and something will be left.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, I am the one who has laid in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation. Whoever believes will not be in haste.”
keyVerse.note: The stone’s primary characteristic is that it has been tested — proven under pressure. The one who builds on it will not need to run in panic. Peter and Paul both identify the stone as Christ, and the New Testament adds the layer of stumbling: the same stone is a rock of offense to those who reject him. Cornerstone or stumbling-block — the stone is the same; the relationship to it makes all the difference.

28.reflection: The leaders of Jerusalem made a “covenant with death” because they could not bear to trust in something invisible when a visible alliance was available. Where in your life are you reaching for a bed that’s too short rather than resting on the tested cornerstone? What would it look like to believe without being in haste?
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley of those overcome with wine! <sup>2</sup>Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest, like a storm of mighty, overflowing waters, he casts down to the earth with his hand. <sup>3</sup>The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot; <sup>4</sup>and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand. <sup>5</sup>In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people, <sup>6</sup>and a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate. <sup>7</sup>These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed by wine, they stagger with strong drink, they reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment. <sup>8</sup>For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left. <sup>9</sup>"To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast? <sup>10</sup>For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little." <sup>11</sup>For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people, <sup>12</sup>to whom he has said, "This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear. <sup>13</sup>And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little, that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken. <sup>14</sup>Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem! <sup>15</sup>Because you have said, "We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement, when the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter"; <sup>16</sup>therefore thus says the Lord GOD, "Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste.' <sup>17</sup>And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter." <sup>18</sup>Then your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand; when the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it. <sup>19</sup>As often as it passes through it will take you; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night; and it will be sheer terror to understand the message. <sup>20</sup>For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in. <sup>21</sup>For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused; to do his deed— strange is his deed! and to work his work— alien is his work! <sup>22</sup>Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of hosts against the whole land. <sup>23</sup>Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech. <sup>24</sup>Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground? <sup>25</sup>When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cumin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border? <sup>26</sup>For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him. <sup>27</sup>Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cumin, but dill is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. <sup>28</sup>Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever; when he drives his cart wheel over it with his horses, he does not crush it. <sup>29</sup>This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.

29.subtitle: Ariel in Distress
29.intro: Overview. Chapter 29 continues the woes with an oracle against Jerusalem, here called Ariel — a word meaning either “lion of God” or “altar hearth,” both rich with associations. The chapter moves through three great movements: the distress and siege of Jerusalem (vv. 1–8), the spiritual blindness of prophets and people (vv. 9–16), and then a surprising turn to hope (vv. 17–24). It contains two of the most-quoted passages in the New Testament from Isaiah: the lip-service condemnation (v. 13) and the potter-clay image (vv. 15–16).

sections.title: Siege and Deliverance
sections.commentary: Ariel adds year to year and celebrates feasts — and yet God himself will besiege it. The city that trusts in its rituals will find God on the side of those who attack it. This is not because God hates Zion but because he is using the siege to bring his people low, to make them speak from the dust in a whisper. And then — suddenly — he will intervene. The attacking nations will become like a dream, like a night vision. Their armies will vanish like a hungry man who dreams of food and wakes still hungry.

sections.title: Spiritual Blindness
sections.commentary:
Astonish yourselves, be astonished; blind yourselves, and be blind. The command is ironic: you have already done this to yourselves. God has poured upon them a spirit of deep sleep; the prophets have become the eyes of the vision, the seers have become the heads of what they see, and it is all covered and sealed. When they hand the sealed book to the literate man he says he cannot read it because it is sealed; when they hand it to the illiterate man he says he cannot read at all. The revelation is present but inaccessible because the heart is closed.

v. 13 — “This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.” Jesus quotes this verse directly against the Pharisees in Matt. 15:8–9, identifying their tradition-keeping as the precise dynamic Isaiah diagnosed. The form of religion has survived while the heart of it has been evacuated.

Verses 15–16 address those who “dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD.” The potter-clay image: does the clay say to the potter, “He did not make me”? Paul develops this image extensively in Romans 9:20–21 in his argument about divine sovereignty. The absurdity of the creature questioning the Creator’s right is the point.

sections.title: The Turn to Hope
sections.commentary: Lebanon will become a fruitful field; the deaf will hear; the blind will see. The meek will obtain fresh joy; the poor will exult in the Holy One of Israel. The tyrant will vanish; the scoffer will be gone; all who watch for evil will be cut off. Jacob will no longer be ashamed. His children will see the work of God’s hands — and those who wandered in spirit will come to understanding. The chapter that began in siege ends in sight and comprehension. The blindness is real and severe, but it is not the final word.

keyVerse.quote: “This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.”
keyVerse.note: Jesus’ application of this verse to the Pharisees makes it timelessly diagnostic. The Pharisees were the most religiously serious people of their generation — and the most thoroughly described by Isaiah’s warning. The danger is not irreligion but religion that has become self-referential: honoring God with forms that protect the heart from actual encounter with him.

29.reflection: Isaiah describes a form of blindness that is self-inflicted: “blind yourselves, and be blind.” The spiritual numbness he diagnoses is not simply ignorance but the accumulated result of not wanting to see clearly. Is there something God has been trying to show you that you have been sealing and covering? What would it cost to open the book?
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round. <sup>2</sup>Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be moaning and lamentation, and she shall be to me like an Ariel. <sup>3</sup>And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you. <sup>4</sup>And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper. <sup>5</sup>But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly, <sup>6</sup>you will be visited by the LORD of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire. <sup>7</sup>And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, all that fight against her and her stronghold and distress her, shall be like a dream, a vision of the night. <sup>8</sup>As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched, so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion. <sup>9</sup>Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink! <sup>10</sup>For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers). <sup>11</sup>And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot, for it is sealed." <sup>12</sup>And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot read." <sup>13</sup>And the Lord said: "Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men, <sup>14</sup>therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden." <sup>15</sup>Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, "Who sees us? Who knows us?" <sup>16</sup>You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, "He has no understanding"? <sup>17</sup>Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest? <sup>18</sup>In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see. <sup>19</sup>The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel. <sup>20</sup>For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off, <sup>21</sup>who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right. <sup>22</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: "Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale. <sup>23</sup>For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel. <sup>24</sup>And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction."

30.subtitle: The Rebellious Children
30.intro: Overview. Chapter 30 contains the fullest treatment in the woes section of Judah’s Egyptian alliance — the plan to go to Pharaoh for protection against Assyria. God calls them “rebellious children” who carry out a plan but not his, who weave a web but not of his Spirit. The chapter is also one of the richest sources of comfort in Isaiah, closing with a remarkable promise about God’s waiting, his gracious response when his people turn, and the coming day when idols will be thrown away like menstrual rags.

sections.title: The Egyptian Alliance
sections.commentary:
Woe to the rebellious children who go to Egypt without asking God, who take refuge in Pharaoh’s protection and shelter in Egypt’s shadow. Isaiah frames this not merely as a political miscalculation but as a spiritual act of unfaith. They have rejected the Holy One of Israel — and chosen horses and chariots instead.

The procession to Egypt is described in detail: they carry their riches on donkeys, their treasures on camels, through the Negeb desert, a land of trouble and anguish — all this to reach a people who cannot help. Egypt is a broken reed, a people who “profit nothing but shame and disgrace.” The oracle is written down as a witness “forever and ever” precisely because the temptation to substitute visible alliances for invisible trust will recur in every generation.

v. 15 — “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.” This is the counter-strategy to the Egyptian alliance. Not military preparation but repentance (returning), not feverish diplomacy but quiet confidence (rest, quietness, trust). The people’s response in verse 16 — “No! We will flee on horses” — is one of the most heartbreaking lines in the whole book.

sections.title: God Waits to Be Gracious
sections.commentary:
The turn in verse 18 is one of the most beautiful sentences in Isaiah: “Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him.” The word waits is extraordinary: God himself is in suspense, watching for the moment he can pour out grace. He is not reluctantly delayed — he is actively oriented toward the moment of return.

The following verses describe what that day will look like: a teacher who will not hide, a voice behind you saying “This is the way, walk in it,” rain for the seed you sow, oxen and donkeys with good fodder, streams of water. And the idols — the gold and silver images, the Egyptian gods they trusted — will be thrown away like a menstrual cloth: “Away with you!” The contempt is the contempt of someone who can finally see clearly what they were holding.

v. 21 — “And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, ‘This is the way, walk in it,’ when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left.” The image of a voice from behind is a guide who walks with you, not a map you consult in advance. The guidance is personal, immediate, relational — not a system but a shepherd.

keyVerse.quote: “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.”
keyVerse.note: The verse is both a promise and a rebuke, because it was rejected. The strength on offer was completely counterintuitive — not cavalry but quietness, not diplomacy but trust. Alistair Begg often noted that God’s strategy always appears inadequate until it is the only strategy left. The tragedy of verse 16 is that Judah never found out whether it worked, because they refused to try.

30.reflection: God is described as waiting to be gracious — not holding back, but oriented toward the moment of your return. What would returning and resting actually look like in whatever you are currently trying to manage by your own strength? And what are the “horses” you keep reaching for instead?
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"Ah, stubborn children," declares the LORD, "who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin; <sup>2</sup>who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt! <sup>3</sup>Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation. <sup>4</sup>For though his officials are at Zoan and his envoys reach Hanes, <sup>5</sup>everyone comes to shame through a people that cannot profit them, that brings neither help nor profit, but shame and disgrace." <sup>6</sup>An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent, they carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them. <sup>7</sup>Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her "Rahab who sits still." <sup>8</sup>And now, go, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever. <sup>9</sup>For they are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD; <sup>10</sup>who say to the seers, "Do not see," and to the prophets, "Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions, <sup>11</sup>leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel." <sup>12</sup>Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel, "Because you despise this word and trust in oppression and perverseness and rely on them, <sup>13</sup>therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse, whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant; <sup>14</sup>and its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern." <sup>15</sup>For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, "In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling, <sup>16</sup>and you said, "No! We will flee upon horses"; therefore you shall flee away; and, "We will ride upon swift steeds"; therefore your pursuers shall be swift. <sup>17</sup>A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain, like a signal on a hill. <sup>18</sup>Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him. <sup>19</sup>For a people shall dwell in Zion, in Jerusalem; you shall weep no more. He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you. <sup>20</sup>And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher. <sup>21</sup>And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, "This is the way, walk in it," when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left. <sup>22</sup>Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver and your gold-plated metal images. You will scatter them as unclean things. You will say to them, "Be gone!" <sup>23</sup>And he will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous. In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures, <sup>24</sup>and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork. <sup>25</sup>And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks running with water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. <sup>26</sup>Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow. <sup>27</sup>Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire; <sup>28</sup>his breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck; to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads astray. <sup>29</sup>You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel. <sup>30</sup>And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones. <sup>31</sup>The Assyrians will be terror-stricken at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod. <sup>32</sup>And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres. Battering them in battle he will fight with them. <sup>33</sup>For a burning place has long been prepared; indeed, for the king it is made ready, its pyre made deep and wide, with fire and wood in abundance; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.

31.subtitle: Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt
31.intro: Overview. Chapter 31 is the sharpest, most compressed of the Egyptian-alliance woes. It drives the contrast between horses and the Holy One to a single question: do you not look to him? But it closes with a promise — Assyria will fall, and not by a human sword — and an image of God as a lion and a mother bird over Jerusalem. The chapter is brief but theologically dense.

sections.title: The Folly of Horses
sections.commentary:
Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD. The critique is not that horses are worthless — they are magnificent military assets. The critique is that Egypt is flesh and not spirit, and God will stretch out his hand and both Egypt and those seeking Egypt’s help will stumble together. The helper and the helped will fall together.

v. 3 — “The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit.” This verse draws the sharpest possible line between trusting in visible power and trusting in the invisible God. The horses are real; the power is real; the military logic is sound. But flesh and spirit operate in different registers, and in a contest between them, flesh will fall.

sections.title: The Lion and the Bird
sections.commentary:
Two images of divine protection, very different in character. First, God as a lion growling over its prey: no noise of shepherds disturbs him; he comes down to fight for Mount Zion. Second, God as birds hovering over Jerusalem: protecting and delivering, passing over and rescuing. The two images together — fierce predator and protective parent — cover the full range of divine care. No threat from below (Assyrian army) and no threat from above (sky) can reach those under his wings.

Assyria’s fall is then announced: he will fall by a sword, not of man; and his officers will be in panic. The army that no human force can stop will be brought down by God alone, without any help from Egypt. This is the practical consequence of God’s sovereignty over military outcomes: the Egyptian alliance was not just wrong theologically but useless strategically.

keyVerse.quote: “The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.”
keyVerse.note: The verse does not disparage military preparation as such but exposes the category error of treating flesh as if it were spirit — of giving to Egypt the trust that belongs only to God. This is the idol-structure in practical form: not a carved image but a military alliance functioning as ultimate security.

31.reflection: The leaders of Judah were not irreligious people — they went to the temple, kept the feasts, consulted prophets. They simply also went to Egypt. The problem was not the absence of religion but its compartmentalization. In what area of your life do you practice religion in one compartment while making practical decisions in another, as if God were not involved?
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD! <sup>2</sup>And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. <sup>3</sup>The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together. <sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me, "As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill. <sup>5</sup>Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it." <sup>6</sup>Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel. <sup>7</sup>For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you. <sup>8</sup>"And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor. <sup>9</sup>His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic," declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

32.subtitle: A King Who Reigns in Righteousness
32.intro: Overview. Chapter 32 pivots from the woes to a vision of what good leadership looks like — a king who reigns in righteousness and princes who rule in justice. It is partly a description of Hezekiah as a contrast to the current failed leaders, and partly a messianic vision of the coming king whose reign will be characterized by true sight, true hearing, and true speech. The chapter also includes a striking oracle to the complacent women of Jerusalem, and closes with a vision of the Spirit poured out.

sections.title: The Righteous King
sections.commentary: In this king’s reign, each person will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, streams of water in a dry place, the shade of a great rock in a weary land. Good governance, Isaiah suggests, creates conditions in which people can actually live and flourish. The eyes of those who see will not be closed; the ears of those who hear will give attention. The social pathology of chapter 29 — blindness, deafness, confusion of moral categories — will be reversed. The fool will no longer be called noble; the scoundrel will no longer be honored. Social recognition will track reality rather than distort it.

sections.title: The Complacent Women
sections.commentary: The oracle against complacent women echoes the warning to the daughters of Zion in chapter 3. They feel secure; the harvest is coming; the vintage will be good. But within a year they will tremble: the harvest will fail, the fruit will not come, the fields and the joyful city will be forsaken. The point is not misogynistic but diagnostic: complacency is the specific danger of those who have been prosperous long enough to forget what prosperity depends on.

sections.title: The Spirit Poured Out
sections.commentary:
Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high. The whole future transformation hinges on this: not better politics or better strategy, but the outpouring of the Spirit. When he comes, the wilderness becomes a fruitful field and the fruitful field is like a forest. Justice dwells in the wilderness; righteousness abides in the fruitful field. The fruit of righteousness will be peace — shalom — and its effect, quietness and trust forever.

v. 17 — “And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever.” The sequence is precise: righteousness produces peace; peace produces quietness; quietness produces trust. It is the reverse of the anxiety spiral. The chapter that began with a king providing shelter closes with a whole people dwelling in shalom because the Spirit has come and righteousness has taken root.

keyVerse.quote: “Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest.”
keyVerse.note: The word until carries the whole weight of chapters 28–32: all the woes, all the warnings, all the distress are the “until” before God acts. This verse is one of Isaiah’s clearest anticipations of Pentecost — the Spirit-outpouring that makes the wilderness bloom.

32.reflection: Isaiah pictures good government as creating conditions where people can hide from the wind and find water in the desert. Whether you are in any kind of leadership — parent, boss, pastor, elder — are you creating those conditions for the people around you? And what would it look like to wait more consciously for the Spirit, rather than trying to produce the fruit of righteousness through effort alone?
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in justice. <sup>2</sup>Each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, like streams of water in a dry place, like the shade of a great rock in a weary land. <sup>3</sup>Then the eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will give attention. <sup>4</sup>The heart of the hasty will understand and know, and the tongue of the stammerers will hasten to speak distinctly. <sup>5</sup>The fool will no more be called noble, nor the scoundrel said to be honorable. <sup>6</sup>For the fool speaks folly, and his heart is busy with iniquity, to practice ungodliness, to utter error concerning the LORD, to leave the craving of the hungry unsatisfied, and to deprive the thirsty of drink. <sup>7</sup>As for the scoundrel— his devices are evil; he plans wicked schemes to ruin the poor with lying words, even when the plea of the needy is right. <sup>8</sup>But he who is noble plans noble things, and on noble things he stands. <sup>9</sup>Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice; you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech. <sup>10</sup>In little more than a year you will shudder, you complacent women; for the grape harvest fails, the fruit harvest will not come. <sup>11</sup>Tremble, you women who are at ease, shudder, you complacent ones; strip, and make yourselves bare, and tie sackcloth around your waist. <sup>12</sup>Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine, <sup>13</sup>for the soil of my people growing up in thorns and briers, yes, for all the joyous houses in the exultant city. <sup>14</sup>For the palace is forsaken, the populous city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys, a pasture of flocks; <sup>15</sup>until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest. <sup>16</sup>Then justice will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness abide in the fruitful field. <sup>17</sup>And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever. <sup>18</sup>My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places. <sup>19</sup>And it will hail when the forest falls down, and the city will be utterly laid low. <sup>20</sup>Happy are you who sow beside all waters, who let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free.

33.subtitle: The LORD Is Our King
33.intro: Overview. Chapter 33 is the last of the woes and serves as a hinge between judgment and hope. It opens with a woe against an unnamed destroyer (Assyria is in view) and moves through prayer, vision, and promise to one of the richest descriptions of God as king in all of Isaiah. The final verses paint a picture of the Jerusalem to come — a city whose inhabitants will never say they are sick, whose sins are forgiven.

sections.title: Prayer in the Crisis
sections.commentary:
The chapter begins with a woe against the destroyer who has not been destroyed — a direct address to Assyria (though not named). When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed. Immediately the community prays: “O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble.” The prayer is the right response to the woe — not military action but return to waiting on God.

The nations who had trusted in Assyrian treaties are now terrified; their envoys wept. The highways are deserted; the covenant is broken; the cities are despised. Lebanon withers; the Jordan languishes. The earth mourns and languishes.

sections.title: The Vision of the King
sections.commentary:
God speaks: “Now I will arise, now I will lift myself up, now I will be exalted.” The three-fold now marks the divine intervention that changes everything. The peoples will be burned; nations will be like lime, cut thorns, consumed in fire. And then the question is asked: who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? The answer is the ethical portrait of the one who walks righteously, speaks uprightly, despises the gain of oppression, shakes his hands free of a bribe — his eyes will see the king in his beauty.

v. 17 — “Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar.” This is the goal of the whole journey — not merely safety from Assyria but vision of the king himself. R.C. Sproul often said that the beatific vision — seeing God face to face — is the consummation of all that redemption aims at. Isaiah puts it as a future that belongs already to those who walk uprightly.

Zion, the city of the LORD, will be a quiet habitation, an unmovable tent whose stakes will never be pulled up. There the LORD will be a place of rivers and broad streams for the people — not the Nile of Egypt but something better. “The LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us.” The triple claim — judge, lawgiver, king — is the assertion that God alone occupies every office that human leaders have failed. And the chapter closes: “No inhabitant will say, ‘I am sick’; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity.”

keyVerse.quote: “For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us.”
keyVerse.note: The threefold office — judge, lawgiver, king — corresponds to the three branches of human governance, but is claimed entirely by God. This is not theocratic politics but eschatological vision: the world as it will be when every human delegation of authority returns to its source. 1 Timothy 6:15 picks up the king language for Christ; James 4:12 the lawgiver-judge.

33.reflection: The one who sees the king in his beauty is described ethically — not by spiritual intensity but by integrity in money, speech, and violence. The vision of God and the ethics of daily life are connected directly. Which of those three areas — money, speech, violence (including contempt) — most needs attention in your own life right now?
33.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed! When you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betraying, they will betray you. <sup>2</sup>O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble. <sup>3</sup>At the tumultuous noise peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, nations are scattered, <sup>4</sup>and your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leaped upon. <sup>5</sup>The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness, <sup>6</sup>and he will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure. <sup>7</sup>Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly. <sup>8</sup>The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man. <sup>9</sup>The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. <sup>10</sup>"Now I will arise," says the LORD, "now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted. <sup>11</sup>You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble; your breath is a fire that will consume you. <sup>12</sup>And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire." <sup>13</sup>Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might. <sup>14</sup>The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: "Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?" <sup>15</sup>He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil, <sup>16</sup>he will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure. <sup>17</sup>Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar. <sup>18</sup>Your heart will muse on the terror: "Where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?" <sup>19</sup>You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue that you cannot understand. <sup>20</sup>Behold Zion, the city of our appointed feasts! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be pulled up, nor will any of its cords be broken. <sup>21</sup>But there the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass. <sup>22</sup>For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us. <sup>23</sup>Your cords hang loose; they cannot hold the mast firm in its place or keep the sail spread out. Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey. <sup>24</sup>And no inhabitant will say, "I am sick"; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity.

34.subtitle: Judgment on the Nations
34.intro: Overview. Chapter 34 is one of the most severe judgment passages in Isaiah, serving as the dark side of the diptych completed by chapter 35. The nations are summoned to hear their sentence; Edom is the representative case — a wasteland of burning pitch and thorns, inhabited by chaos creatures. The desolation is total and permanent. The vision is eschatological in scope: it is what the end of human rebellion looks like before the new creation blooms in the next chapter.

sections.title: The Day of the LORD’s Vengeance
sections.commentary:
All nations, all peoples — draw near and hear. God is enraged against them all; their slain will be cast out, and the mountains will flow with their blood. The host of heaven will rot; the skies roll up like a scroll; all the starry host will fall like leaves from a fig tree. The cosmic-dismantling imagery here feeds directly into Revelation 6:13–14, where John uses the same images for the opening of the sixth seal. Isaiah is not predicting an astronomical event but using the only language adequate to describe the uncreating of the order that has been made to serve rebellion.

v. 4 — “All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll.” Jesus uses the same collapsing-sky language in Matt. 24:29 for the events surrounding Jerusalem’s fall, and John uses it for the last judgment. Isaiah establishes the grammar; the New Testament applies it with increasing specificity.

The specific focus falls on Edom, Israel’s perennial enemy and twin-brother nation, as the type-case of those under divine wrath. God has a day of vengeance and a year of recompense for Edom’s cause — the violence done to Jacob will be answered.

sections.title: The Desolate Inheritance
sections.commentary:
Edom’s streams will be turned to pitch, its soil to sulfur; it will not be quenched night or day. The owls and ravens, jackals and ostriches, the screech owl and the arrow snake will make their home there. It will be called “No Kingdom There.” God’s line and plumb line will be stretched over it for chaos and emptiness — the tools of creation used for de-creation.

The chapter closes with a challenge: seek and read from the book of the LORD. Not one of these creatures will be missing; not one will lack its mate. His Spirit has gathered them; his hand has sorted them. God’s word has prescribed the desolation as precisely as any survey. The chaos is not accidental but ordained.

keyVerse.quote: “Seek and read from the book of the LORD: not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them.”
keyVerse.note: Even the desolation is governed by a book — by God’s word precisely applied. This is not chaos but ordered judgment. The same God who speaks creation into existence speaks desolation into a place that has refused him. The book-of-the-LORD motif connects to Isaiah 8:16–20 and ultimately to the Book of Life in Revelation.

34.reflection: Chapter 34 is difficult to read — the severity is comprehensive and without relief until chapter 35. But Isaiah places it immediately before the greatest vision of healing and return in the book. The comfort of chapter 35 lands differently if you have stood in the desolation of chapter 34 first. What aspects of the Bible’s severity do you tend to skip past? What does reading them in full do to your understanding of what grace actually costs?
34.text: <sup>1</sup>Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it. <sup>2</sup>For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter. <sup>3</sup>Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood. <sup>4</sup>All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from the fig tree. <sup>5</sup>For my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction. <sup>6</sup>The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood; it is gorged with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom. <sup>7</sup>Wild oxen shall fall with them, and young steers with the mighty bulls. Their land shall drink its fill of blood, and their soil shall be gorged with fat. <sup>8</sup>For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. <sup>9</sup>And the streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch. <sup>10</sup>Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it forever and ever. <sup>11</sup>But the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness. <sup>12</sup>Its nobles— there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing. <sup>13</sup>Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches. <sup>14</sup>And wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place. <sup>15</sup>There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate. <sup>16</sup>Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them. <sup>17</sup>He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with the line; they shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it.

35.subtitle: The Highway of Holiness
35.intro: Overview. Chapter 35 is among the most luminous passages in all of Scripture — the other half of the diptych with chapter 34, and the first foretaste of the great vision of restoration in chapters 40–66. The wilderness blooms; the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, the mute sing; a highway appears in the desert called the Way of Holiness; and the ransomed return with everlasting joy. Jesus reads from this chapter to answer John the Baptist’s question about whether he is the one who was to come (Matt. 11:5).

sections.title: The Wilderness Blooms
sections.commentary:
The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus. Lebanon’s glory, Carmel’s majesty, Sharon’s beauty — the most fertile and famous landscapes of the land will be seen in the wilderness that was barren. The creation itself participates in the reversal. Strengthen the weak hands, make firm the feeble knees; say to those with an anxious heart: “Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come.”

vv. 5–6 — “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy.” Jesus quotes these verses in Matt. 11:5 as evidence that the kingdom has arrived: the miracles are not random acts of kindness but the specific signs Isaiah listed as markers of the new age. When Jesus heals, he is enacting the chapter.

Waters break forth in the wilderness; streams in the desert. The burning sand becomes a pool; the thirsty ground springs of water. Even the dwelling place of jackals — the haunt of the chaos creatures of chapter 34 — becomes a place of grass and reeds. The precise reversal of the previous chapter is not accidental.

sections.title: The Way of Holiness
sections.commentary:
A highway shall be there — the Way of Holiness. The unclean shall not pass over it; no lion shall be there, no ravenous beast. It is for those who walk on the way, even fools (simple ones) shall not err. The image of the highway cutting through the wilderness is the central metaphor of Isaiah 40–55 (“make straight in the desert a highway for our God”) and appears here in its first full form. The road is designed not for experts but for the redeemed: no special competence required, no predators waiting, just the path home.

And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. The chapter closes the same way chapter 25 did — with tears ended, joy permanent, the destination reached. These are not metaphors of spiritual improvement; they are the promise of arrival.

keyVerse.quote: “And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it… the redeemed shall walk there.”
keyVerse.note: The Way of Holiness is the image John picks up for the New Jerusalem: nothing unclean will enter it (Rev. 21:27). But Isaiah adds what John implies: it is not the pure who travel the road — it is the redeemed, the ransomed, even the simple.
