Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your heritage. <sup>18</sup>Your holy people held possession for a little while; our adversaries have trampled down your sanctuary. <sup>19</sup>We have become like those over whom you have never ruled, like those who are not called by your name.

64.subtitle: Oh That You Would Rend the Heavens
64.intro: Overview. Chapter 64 is the climax of the communal lament begun in 63:7. It opens with a cry for divine intervention — “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down!” — and moves through honest confession to a final question left hanging before God: “Will you keep silent and afflict us so severely?” The prayer does not end with an answer; it ends with an open appeal to the one who is Potter and Father.

sections.title: Rend the Heavens
sections.commentary:
Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence. From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him. Paul quotes verse 4 in 1 Cor. 2:9 as the description of what God has revealed through the Spirit: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, God has prepared for those who love him.” The prayer for God to come down anticipates the incarnation — God rending the heavens in the most literal way.

We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away. There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you. The confession moves from polished garment imagery to leaf-fading decay. The community has no ground to stand on but the character of the one they are addressing.

v. 6 — “We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.” The Hebrew behind “polluted garment” is among the strongest expressions of uncleanness in the Torah. The confession is not measured; it is total. All righteous deeds — not just the obvious failures but the best attempts at righteousness — fall short of the holiness they are measured against.

sections.title: The Potter and His Clay
sections.commentary: But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand. Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people. The prayer closes with five questions that leave the community in suspense before God: will you restrain yourself? Will you keep silent and afflict us so severely? The prayer does not manufacture its own resolution. It ends where many of our prayers need to end — with the appeal delivered, the outcome held in God’s hands, and the people still on their knees.

keyVerse.quote: “But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.”
keyVerse.note: The potter-clay image has appeared throughout Isaiah as a warning against human presumption (29:16; 45:9). Here it becomes a resource for prayer: the very creatureliness that makes us answerable to God is also the ground of our appeal to him. We have no independent standing — but we are his clay, his work, and the potter does not discard what his hands have made.

64.reflection: The prayer in chapter 64 ends without an answer — the community is still in suspense before God. This is not a model of weak faith but of honest prayer: not every prayer resolves before you close it. Is there a prayer you have been trying to resolve yourself rather than letting it end openly before God? What would it look like to lay it down as the community does here — completely, and without manufacturing your own answer?
64.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence— <sup>2</sup>as when fire kindles brushwood and the fire causes water to boil— to make your name known to your adversaries, and that the nations might tremble at your presence! <sup>3</sup>When you did awesome things that we did not look for, you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence. <sup>4</sup>From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him. <sup>5</sup>You meet him who joyfully works righteousness, those who remember you in your ways. Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? <sup>6</sup>We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away. <sup>7</sup>There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities. <sup>8</sup>But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand. <sup>9</sup>Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people. <sup>10</sup>Your holy cities have become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation. <sup>11</sup>Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised you, has been burned by fire, and all our pleasant places have become ruins. <sup>12</sup>Will you restrain yourself at these things, O LORD? Will you keep silent, and afflict us so severely?

65.subtitle: Behold, I Create New Heavens and a New Earth
65.intro: Overview. Chapter 65 is God’s answer to the anguished prayer of chapters 63–64. He addresses both the rebels and the servants: judgment for those who persistently chose their own way; and for those who sought him, the most extensive description of the new creation in all of Isaiah. The chapter contains the great vision of the peaceable kingdom extended to all of creation — no crying, no infant mortality, no labor wasted, no animal killing — and closes with God’s declaration that what is past will not be remembered.

sections.title: Two Destinies
sections.commentary:
I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, “Here I am, here I am.” Paul quotes verses 1–2 in Romans 10:20–21 as the description of God’s relationship to the Gentiles (ready to be found) and to Israel (outstretched hands). The God of Isaiah is the seeking God: before the people asked, he called; before they sought, he stretched out his hands.

But the rebels — who sacrifice in gardens, burn incense on bricks, sit in tombs, eat pig’s flesh — will receive what their deeds deserve. They said “Keep to yourself; do not come near me, for I am too holy for you” — the supreme irony: the unholy claiming holiness to exclude the holy God. The servants, by contrast, will be given a different name: God will be called the God of faithfulness, and the former troubles will be forgotten.

sections.title: The New Creation
sections.commentary:
For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. Be glad and rejoice forever in what I create. The vision that follows is detailed and domestic: no more weeping, no more infant mortality, the person who dies at a hundred will be called young, they shall build houses and inhabit them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity — the two great losses of Deuteronomy’s curse (Deut. 28:30, 41) are directly reversed.

v. 24 — “Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear.” This is the answer to the unanswered prayer of chapter 64: in the new creation, the gap between calling and answering is zero. The community that ended chapter 64 with open questions held before a silent heaven will inhabit a world where the answer comes before the question is finished.

The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox. The peaceable kingdom of chapter 11 returns in the new creation context: not a temporary truce but a permanent ontological change in what the creatures are. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain, says the LORD.

keyVerse.quote: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.”
keyVerse.note: Revelation 21:1 quotes this verse almost exactly: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” The new creation is not the destruction of creation but its transformation — the same creation, purged of everything that corrupted it. “Former things shall not be remembered” is not amnesia but healing: what will make the former things forgettable is not that they are erased but that they are overwhelmed by joy.

65.theology: New Creation. Isaiah 65:17–25 is the fullest Old Testament vision of the telos — the goal — of redemptive history. It is not escape from the material world but its renewal: houses built and inhabited, vineyards planted and enjoyed, infant mortality ended, predation abolished. Reformed theology has insisted against Gnosticism and against pure “heaven-escape” that the resurrection is bodily and the new creation is physical. This vision is why. The new creation is this creation redeemed, not a different creation substituted for this one. N.T. Wright calls this “life after life after death” — and its biblical foundation is here in Isaiah 65.
65.reflection: God says the former things will not be remembered — not because they are denied but because joy will overwhelm them. What “former things” are you carrying right now that feel permanent? What would it mean to let the new creation vision recalibrate your sense of what is permanent and what is temporary? And what is the most specific thing you are most looking forward to about the world this chapter describes?
65.text: <sup>1</sup>I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, "Here I am, here I am," to a nation that was not called by my name. <sup>2</sup>I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices; <sup>3</sup>a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks; <sup>4</sup>who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels; <sup>5</sup>who say, "Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you." These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day. <sup>6</sup>Behold, it is written before me: "I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap <sup>7</sup>both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together, says the LORD; because they made offerings on the mountains and insulted me on the hills, I will measure into their lap payment for their former deeds." <sup>8</sup>Thus says the LORD: "As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all. <sup>9</sup>I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah inheritors of my mountains; my chosen shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there. <sup>10</sup>Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me. <sup>11</sup>But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny, <sup>12</sup>I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter, because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in." <sup>13</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; <sup>14</sup>behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit. <sup>15</sup>You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name. <sup>16</sup>So that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes. <sup>17</sup>For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. <sup>18</sup>But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness. <sup>19</sup>I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress. <sup>20</sup>No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed. <sup>21</sup>They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. <sup>22</sup>They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands. <sup>23</sup>They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them. <sup>24</sup>Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear. <sup>25</sup>The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain," says the LORD.

66.subtitle: This Is the One to Whom I Will Look
66.intro: Overview. Chapter 66 is Isaiah’s final word, and it holds nothing back. God asks: where is the house you would build for me? Heaven is my throne; the earth is my footstool. The one he looks to is not the grand temple-builder but the one who is humble and contrite and trembles at his word. The chapter moves through birth-like imagery of Zion’s sudden deliverance, the judgment of the rebellious, and closes with the greatest gathering of all nations in Scripture — including some as priests and Levites — and the permanent worship of the redeemed. The final verse is unresolved: the corpses of those who rebelled will be seen; their worm does not die. The book ends holding both eternal life and eternal judgment before the reader.

sections.title: The One Who Trembles at My Word
sections.commentary:
Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me? The question demolishes every project of confining God in human-made spaces. He made everything; everything is already his address. But then: this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. The cosmic vision contracts to a single quality: trembling at the word.

v. 2 — “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.” The enormous God — whose throne is heaven — looks at one specific kind of person. Not the grand, not the theologically sophisticated, not the ritually accomplished: the humble and trembling. This is the New Testament’s “poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3) and the Publican’s prayer (Luke 18:13). The character of the look is not pity but delight.

sections.title: The Birth and the Deliverance
sections.commentary:
A sound of uproar from the city, a sound from the temple, the sound of the LORD rendering recompense to his enemies. Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. The birth metaphor for the restoration is instantaneous and overwhelming: not a long recovery but a sudden arrival.

Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy. As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem. The comforting of chapter 40 is here at the end, in its fullest personal form: God as mother, the comforted as child, Jerusalem as the home where the comfort happens.

sections.title: The Final Gathering
sections.commentary:
For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory. God will send survivors to the nations — to Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, Javan, the coastlands — and they shall declare his glory among the nations. And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD. Some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites.

The inclusion of Gentiles as priests and Levites is breathtaking in context: the offices reserved for a single tribe in Israel will be given to those from the farthest nations. This is the fulfillment of chapter 56’s promise and the ground of 1 Peter 2:9: “you are a royal priesthood, a holy nation.”

And from new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD. The book ends with unending worship — all flesh, every cycle of time, before God. And then, immediately: they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh. The book of Isaiah ends holding eternity open in both directions: unending worship and unending judgment, side by side, without resolution, before the reader.

keyVerse.quote: “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word.”
keyVerse.note: The cosmic God — whose throne is heaven and footstool the earth — focuses his gaze on one kind of person. Not the magnificent, not the impressive, not the doctrinally complete: the humble and trembling. This is the first beatitude in Old Testament form. It is also the conclusion Isaiah has been building toward: after 66 chapters about the incomparable God, the question is not what house will satisfy him but what heart — and the answer is the broken, attentive one.

66.theology: Eternal Life and Eternal Judgment. Isaiah 66:24 — “their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched” — is the Old Testament text Jesus quotes three times in Mark 9:44–48 as the description of hell. The book of Isaiah ends with eternal life (all flesh worshiping forever) and eternal judgment (worm and fire that do not die) placed side by side without resolution. Reformed theology has always insisted that both are real and both are permanent: universalism fails on Isaiah 66:24, and despair fails on 66:23. The response the book calls for is the response of verse 2: humility, contrition, and trembling at the word of the God who holds both futures in his hand.
66.reflection: Isaiah ends not with a resolution but with two destinations placed before the reader. The worm and fire of verse 24 are visible from the place of endless worship in verse 23 — the redeemed will forever know what they were saved from. After 66 chapters of the incomparable God — his holiness, his judgment, his grace, his suffering Servant, his new creation — what is your response? Is it trembling at his word? Humble faith? The book leaves the question with you, as every prophet must.
66.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me, and what is the place of my rest? <sup>2</sup>All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, declares the LORD. But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word. <sup>3</sup>He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog's neck; he who presents a grain offering, like one who offers pig's blood; he who makes a memorial offering of frankincense, like one who blesses an idol. These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations; <sup>4</sup>I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in." <sup>5</sup>Hear the word of the LORD, you who tremble at his word: "Your brothers who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake have said, 'Let the LORD be glorified, that we may see your joy'; but it is they who shall be put to shame. <sup>6</sup>The sound of an uproar from the city! A sound from the temple! The sound of the LORD, rendering recompense to his enemies! <sup>7</sup>Before she was in labor she gave birth; before her pain came upon her she delivered a son. <sup>8</sup>Who has heard such a thing? Who has seen such things? Shall a land be born in one day? Shall a nation be brought forth in one moment? For as soon as Zion was in labor she brought forth her children. <sup>9</sup>Shall I bring to the point of birth and not cause to bring forth?" says the LORD; "shall I, who cause to bring forth, shut the womb?" says your God. <sup>10</sup>Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad for her, all you who love her; rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her; <sup>11</sup>that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance." <sup>12</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the nations like an overflowing stream; and you shall nurse, you shall be carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees. <sup>13</sup>As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice; your bones shall flourish like the grass; and the hand of the LORD shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies. <sup>15</sup>For behold, the LORD will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. <sup>16</sup>For by fire will the LORD enter into judgment, and by his sword, with all flesh; and those slain by the LORD shall be many. <sup>17</sup>Those who sanctify and purify themselves to go into the gardens, following one in the midst, eating pig's flesh and the abomination and mice, shall come to an end together, declares the LORD. <sup>18</sup>For I know their works and their thoughts, and the time is coming to gather all nations and tongues. And they shall come and shall see my glory, <sup>19</sup>and I will set a sign among them. And from them I will send survivors to the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, who draw the bow, to Tubal and Javan, to the coastlands far away, that have not heard my fame or seen my glory. And they shall declare my glory among the nations. <sup>20</sup>And they shall bring all your brothers from all the nations as an offering to the LORD, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and on dromedaries, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the LORD, just as the Israelites bring their grain offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD. <sup>21</sup>And some of them also I will take for priests and for Levites, says the LORD. <sup>22</sup>For as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall remain before me, says the LORD, so shall your offspring and your name remain. <sup>23</sup>From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh shall come to worship before me, declares the LORD. <sup>24</sup>And they shall go out and look on the dead bodies of the men who have rebelled against me. For their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."

0.subtitle: Introduction
0.intro:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem through the reigns of four kings — Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah — from around 740 to 700 BC. His call came in the year that King Uzziah died (chapter 6): a vision of the Lord high and lifted up, the seraphim crying Holy, holy, holy, and the commission to speak a word that most would refuse to hear. From that moment Isaiah became the greatest of the writing prophets — and this book became what Luther called “the fifth Gospel.”

The book divides naturally into two great halves. Chapters 1–39 address the Assyrian crisis: God’s judgment on Israel and Judah, the fate of the surrounding nations, and the demand for faith in the Holy One rather than military alliance. Chapters 40–66 address a people in Babylonian exile, not yet experienced but anticipated by prophetic foresight: comfort, homecoming, and the glorious emergence of the Servant who bears the sin of the world. The two halves share the same vocabulary, the same theology, and the same God — against all critical attempts to divide them.

The name of God that defines the book is the Holy One of Israel. It appears twenty-six times in Isaiah and only six times in the rest of the Old Testament. Holiness is not merely moral purity; it is the utter otherness of God, his transcendent glory that both terrifies and draws. Everything in Isaiah — judgment and comfort, wrath and mercy — flows from who this God is. The prophet’s task is to make the Holy One of Israel known.

The four Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) form the theological heartbeat of the second half. They move from the Servant’s gentle justice to his voluntary suffering — despised, crushed, pierced for our transgressions — and his ultimate vindication. The New Testament quotes or alludes to Isaiah more than any other Old Testament book. Jesus opened his ministry with Isaiah 61. Philip expounded Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian on the road. John saw Isaiah 6 as a vision of Christ’s glory.

To preach Isaiah is to preach the whole gospel in its Old Testament register: the holiness that makes sin impossible to ignore, the grace that makes forgiveness inconceivably costly, and the glory of a God who will not rest until his purposes fill the earth as the waters cover the sea. Sproul said that no book of Scripture humbled him more. No book of Scripture delighted him more either. Both responses flow from the same source: the Holy One of Israel, sovereign, saving, and surpassingly glorious.
